stories.title: The Map That Looked the Wrong Way

pages.text: The summer Lina Al-Harbi turned sixteen, her uncle Saeed offered her a job that sounded, at first, unbearably dull: cataloguing dusty objects in the old merchant house he was restoring in Jeddah's historic district. The building, with its coral-stone walls and carved wooden rawashin, had stood for nearly two centuries, and Uncle Saeed spoke about it the way other people spoke about a beloved relative. Its greatest treasure was a hand-drawn chart of the Red Sea coast, made by a pearl merchant who had sailed these waters long before anyone had heard of satellites. Lina, who secretly preferred crime novels to history books, had expected to be bored within a week. Instead, by the end of the first month, she had grown strangely attached to the faded chart, with its delicate islands and the tiny crescent-shaped ink blot in its top-left corner. "Every flaw tells a story," her uncle liked to say, and she had begun to believe him.

On the morning the chart was due to be photographed for a national exhibition, Uncle Saeed unlocked the display room and stopped dead in the doorway. Nothing appeared to be missing; the glass case was intact, the lock untouched, and the chart lay exactly where it always had. Yet he stood frozen for so long that Lina finally asked whether he was feeling unwell. "It's the paper," he murmured, leaning so close that his breath clouded the glass. "It's too clean, too even, as if someone has aged it with tea rather than time." Within an hour, a conservator had confirmed his fear: the chart in the case was an expert forgery, and the original had vanished without a trace.

Only three people besides the family had been given access to the display room that week, and Uncle Saeed reluctantly listed them at the kitchen table. There was Mr. Hamdan, the elderly carpenter repairing the wooden balconies, who had worked on the house for years and treated every beam as though it were made of glass. There was Tariq, the quiet young assistant who had designed the exhibition catalogue and was rarely seen without his laptop. And there was Dr. Rania Khalil, a respected conservator from Cairo, who had arrived a fortnight earlier with a heavy aluminium case full of brushes, solvents and magnifying lenses. "I would trust any of them with my life," her uncle said wearily, rubbing his temples. "Which, I suppose, is precisely the problem."

The police officer who came that afternoon was polite but clearly unconvinced that the case would be solved quickly. Forgeries of this quality, he explained, were usually commissioned by private collectors abroad, and by the time anyone noticed, the originals had often crossed several borders. Lina listened from the corner of the room, her notebook balanced on her knee, determined not to miss a single detail. She found herself studying the fake more closely than she had ever studied the real thing, as though it might confess if she stared at it long enough. The coastline was flawless, the handwriting convincing, the islands perfectly placed. Then her eyes drifted to the top corner, and her heart gave a sudden, painful jolt.

The little crescent-shaped blot was there, as it should have been, but it was in the top-right corner instead of the top-left. For a moment Lina doubted her own memory, wondering whether weeks of staring at the chart had simply muddled her. Yet she had sketched that blot in her notebook on her very first day, and when she flicked back through the pages, there it was, unmistakably on the left. Why would a forger who had copied every island and every letter so precisely make such a careless mistake? She recalled something her grandmother used to say whenever someone told a half-truth: "A mirror never lies, but it always shows things the wrong way round." Slowly, an idea began to take shape.

That evening, Lina asked Tariq to show her every version of the exhibition catalogue he had produced. He seemed puzzled, but he fetched a box from his car and laid out the finished copies alongside a slim, spiral-bound booklet. "That's one of the proof copies," he explained, slightly embarrassed. "The printer accidentally reversed the photograph of the chart, so the whole image came out as a mirror image, and we had to correct it before the final run." Lina's pulse quickened as she turned to the page in question, and there, in the top-right corner, sat the crescent-shaped blot. The forger had not worked from the original at all, but from this faulty photograph, and had carefully rewritten the text the right way round without noticing that the drawing itself had been flipped.

"How many of these proof copies exist?" Lina asked, trying to keep her voice steady. Tariq frowned and counted on his fingers: one had stayed with the printer, one belonged to Uncle Saeed, and the third had been sent to Dr. Rania so that she could check the technical descriptions. The printer's copy, a quick phone call revealed, was still locked in his office in Riyadh. Uncle Saeed's copy lay untouched on his desk, its pages still stiff and unopened. That left only one person who could have possessed the reversed image long enough to copy it with such painstaking care. Lina closed her notebook, realising with a sinking feeling that the most charming guest in the house might also be the most dangerous.

Lina knew that an accusation without proof would be both foolish and unfair, so she shared her theory only with her uncle and the police officer. To her relief, neither of them laughed; the officer, in fact, looked at her with newfound respect. The next morning, Dr. Rania announced that urgent work required her to return to Cairo earlier than planned, and she began packing her aluminium case with unusual haste. When the officer politely asked to inspect it, she protested that her instruments were delicate and that any interference would be an insult to her professional reputation. Her objections, however, only made him more determined. He lifted out the trays of brushes and bottles one by one until his fingers found a thin seam along the base of the case.

Beneath a false bottom, wrapped in acid-free tissue, lay the original chart, its crescent-shaped blot sitting proudly in the top-left corner. Dr. Rania said nothing at first, her composure crumbling as the evidence was photographed and sealed. Eventually she admitted that a foreign collector had offered her a fortune for the chart, and that she had spent many nights in her hotel room reproducing it from the proof copy. "It was perfect," she whispered bitterly, "except for one detail I never thought anyone would notice." Uncle Saeed shook his head, more saddened than angry, and remarked that the house had been guarding its secrets far longer than she had been trying to steal them. Lina, for her part, felt no triumph, only a quiet relief that the chart had come home.

A week later, the restored chart was returned to its case, and the exhibition opened to crowds of visitors who had read about the theft in the newspapers. Beside the chart, Uncle Saeed placed a small card describing how a sixteen-year-old intern had noticed what experts had overlooked. Lina found the attention rather embarrassing, but she could not help smiling when a group of younger students gathered around the case, searching eagerly for the famous blot. Her uncle joined her at the window as the sun sank over the old rooftops, turning the coral stone the colour of honey. "So," he teased, "is history still unbearably dull?" Lina laughed and admitted that she had been wrong, because history, it turned out, was simply a mystery that was waiting for someone patient enough to read it properly.

questions.q: What first made Uncle Saeed suspect that the chart in the case was not the original?
options: The paper looked too clean and evenly aged
The glass case had been broken
The ink blot was missing completely

questions.q: Why was the crescent-shaped blot in the wrong corner on the forgery?
options: The forger wanted to leave a secret signature
The forger copied a photograph that had been printed as a mirror image
Dr. Rania had damaged the original chart while cleaning it

questions.q: In the story, the word "painstaking" (page 7) is closest in meaning to:
options: quick and careless
extremely careful and thorough
painful and dangerous

questions.q: Why did Lina share her theory only with her uncle and the police officer?
options: She was afraid Dr. Rania would hurt her
She wanted to take all the credit herself
She knew accusing someone without proof would be foolish and unfair

questions.q: What can we infer about how Lina changed during the story?
options: She began to see history as something exciting, like a mystery
She decided to become a police officer immediately
She lost interest in crime novels completely

pages.text: In Jeddah, everyone had a favourite hero, and most people would argue about theirs until the tea went cold. Some admired Blaze, who could wrap himself in fire and streak across the sky like a meteor, while others swore by the Tide Sisters, who could pull water out of thin air. Sixteen-year-old Faris Al-Harbi had a power too, though he had never told a soul, and he suspected that nobody would have been impressed if he had. Ever since his fourteenth birthday, he had been able to rewind time by exactly one second. Not two seconds, not a minute, and certainly not long enough to undo a bad exam result. So far, the greatest achievement of his secret career had been rescuing his mother's favourite glass from certain destruction on the kitchen floor.

That summer, Faris took a job at a cramped repair shop near the old harbour, owned by a quiet man everyone called Uncle Saeed. The shop smelled of oil and cardamom, and its shelves were crammed with radios, fans and engines that other people had given up on. On his third day, Faris knocked a box of screws off the counter, rewound the moment, and caught it before it fell. When he looked up, Uncle Saeed was watching him over his reading glasses with an expression that was impossible to read. "You did that twice," the old man said calmly. "The first time, the box hit the floor."

Faris's heart was pounding so hard he could barely get the words out. "Nobody can see it," he stammered. "When I go back, nobody remembers what happened." Uncle Saeed smiled and pulled a faded photograph from a drawer, showing a younger version of himself holding up a collapsing bridge with his bare hands. "Thirty years ago, they called me the Anchor," he explained. "I can't lift bridges any more, but my power left me with a certain sensitivity to people bending the rules of the world." Faris stared at the photograph, torn between excitement and embarrassment that his own ability was so pitifully small by comparison.

"Mine is useless," Faris admitted that evening, as they closed the shutters. "Blaze can fly; I can fix a mistake that lasted as long as a sneeze." Uncle Saeed shook his head, as though he had heard this complaint many times before from people who should have known better. "A second is a very long time," he said, "if you know exactly what to do with it." He went on to explain that strength had never been his real gift; what had kept him alive was paying attention. "Most people waste their seconds because they are not looking properly," he added. "Learn to notice everything, and your second will become worth more than a whole hour of someone else's."

Over the following weeks, the training was nothing like Faris had imagined. Instead of dramatic exercises, Uncle Saeed made him sit by the window and describe every car, every pedestrian and every bird that passed. He had to predict which customer would drop their keys, which shelf would wobble, and which engine would cough before it started. At first, Faris found it maddeningly dull and wondered whether he had bitten off more than he could chew. Gradually, however, he realised that he was beginning to see the world as a series of tiny, connected moments, each one a door that could be opened or closed. Had anyone told him at the start of the summer that staring out of a window could be exhausting, he would have laughed.

The test came without warning on a blistering afternoon in August, when they were delivering spare parts to the port. A sandstorm swept in from the desert so suddenly that the sky turned the colour of rust within minutes. Through the swirling dust, Faris saw a massive crane lurching sideways, a steel container swinging wildly from its cable above a group of workers. A sharp crack echoed across the docks as one of the crane's supports gave way. Moments later, Blaze shot overhead in a streak of orange flame, but the furious wind kept throwing him off course. "He can't get close enough!" Uncle Saeed shouted, gripping his injured knee. "Someone needs to reach the control cabin."

Faris was already running before he had made a conscious decision to move. The ladder to the cabin was slippery with sand, and halfway up, his foot slid off a rung and he felt himself falling. He snapped back one second, gripped the rail more firmly, and kept climbing. Inside the cabin, the operator was slumped against the window, dazed by a blow to the head, and the control panel was a confusing mess of blinking lights. Faris pulled the largest lever, only to watch the container swing even more violently towards the workers. Back he went, one second, and tried another switch, and then another, each failure teaching him something new.

With every rewind, a sharper pain stabbed behind his eyes, as though his own mind were protesting against the strain. He forced himself to slow down and do what Uncle Saeed had taught him: stop panicking and start noticing. That was when he spotted it, a small red brake handle that had been jammed halfway by a twisted piece of metal. He worked out that if he released it at the exact moment the container swung away from the workers, it would drop onto the empty ground beside them. On his first attempt he was too early, and on his second he was too late. On the third, against all odds, the timing was perfect.

The container slammed onto the concrete with a deafening crash, sending up a cloud of dust but harming no one. At the same instant, Blaze finally broke through the wind and seized the snapped cable, holding the crane steady until the storm began to die down. The workers burst into cheers, and within minutes, crowds were filming the famous hero as he landed beside the wreckage. "Who released the brake?" Blaze asked, looking around in confusion. "I couldn't have done this alone." Faris, who was helping the injured operator down the ladder, simply kept his head down and said nothing at all.

That night, Faris sat in the repair shop with a terrible headache and a glass of sweet tea that Uncle Saeed had insisted he drink. "You could have told them," the old man remarked, his eyes twinkling. "You might have been on every screen in the kingdom by now." Faris shrugged and admitted that, for once, he had not wanted to be seen; he had only wanted everyone to get home safely. A week later, there was a knock at the shop door, and Blaze himself stood there, holding a broken radio and wearing a slightly sheepish smile. "I've heard," he said, "that this is where people learn to pay attention." Faris glanced at the clock on the wall and grinned, because he finally understood that a single second, used well, could change everything.

questions.q: How did Uncle Saeed first discover Faris's secret power?
options: He noticed that Faris had caught a falling box after it had already hit the floor once.
He saw Faris rescue his mother's favourite glass in the kitchen.
Blaze told him about a boy who could control time.

questions.q: What does Uncle Saeed mean when he says, "A second is a very long time if you know exactly what to do with it"?
options: Faris should practise until he can rewind for longer periods.
Careful observation can make even a small power extremely valuable.
Time passes more slowly for people who have superpowers.

questions.q: In the story, the phrase "bitten off more than he could chew" suggests that Faris felt...
options: hungry after long hours of training.
he had taken on something too difficult for him.
bored because the work was far too easy.

questions.q: What finally allowed Faris to save the workers at the port?
options: He pulled the largest lever as soon as he entered the cabin.
He flew to the crane with Blaze and held the cable.
He noticed a jammed red brake handle and released it at the right moment.

questions.q: Why do you think Blaze visited the repair shop at the end of the story?
options: He wanted to learn the skill of paying attention that had helped save the day.
He only needed someone to repair his radio as quickly as possible.
He wanted to publicly accuse Faris of interfering in his rescue.

stories.title: The Typo That Told the Truth

pages.text: When the headmaster read out the shortlist for the National Student Essay Prize, Yusuf Al-Harbi almost missed his own name, because he was busy trying to remember whether he had left his calculator in the chemistry lab. It was only when the boys around him started thumping his shoulders that the words sank in. His essay, "The Palm That Remembered," was about his grandfather's date farm in Al-Ahsa and the slow, patient work of keeping something alive through drought. He had written it over three months, in stolen hours after maths revision, rewriting the opening paragraph so many times that his mother had joked he should frame the discarded versions. Now, out of more than four thousand entries from across the Kingdom, it was one of only six to reach the final. For the rest of the day, Yusuf walked the corridors in a kind of pleasant daze.

The daze lasted precisely nine days. On a grey Tuesday morning, he was called to the office of Mr Kamal, the deputy head, a man known for his dry humour and his habit of polishing his glasses whenever he was about to deliver bad news. He was polishing them furiously. "Yusuf, I'm afraid the competition committee has raised a serious concern," he said, sliding a printed page across the desk. It was a blog post, published under the name "WiseWords_Daily," and its first paragraph was almost word for word the opening of Yusuf's essay. "They are suggesting that you may have copied it," Mr Kamal continued quietly, "and until the matter is resolved, your place in the final has been suspended."

News, as it invariably does in a school of six hundred teenage boys, travelled faster than any official announcement. By lunchtime, Yusuf could feel eyes following him across the courtyard, and conversations would trail off awkwardly whenever he approached. Some boys were openly sympathetic, while others seemed to relish the drama, as if a scandal were more entertaining than a success. The comment that stung most came from Hamad Al-Qahtani, his long-standing rival in every debate and every exam. "Funny how the best essays always seem to appear online first," Hamad remarked to nobody in particular, loud enough to be heard. Yusuf said nothing, but that evening he sat at his desk staring at the blog post until the words blurred, wondering how his most personal piece of writing could possibly belong to a stranger.

It was his grandfather, visiting from Al-Ahsa for the weekend, who finally coaxed the story out of him. The old man listened without interrupting, turning his prayer beads slowly between his fingers. "When a farmer is accused of stealing water from his neighbour's well," he said at last, "he does not shout. He shows the channels he dug himself, and the mud still on his hands." Yusuf frowned, unsure whether he was being given advice or a riddle. "Your essay did not appear out of thin air, my son," his grandfather added with a gentle smile. "Somewhere, there are footprints. Go and find them."

So Yusuf began to retrace his steps with almost obsessive care. He opened the school's online drive and found every draft he had ever saved, each one carrying a date and time that no one could have altered. The earliest version, a clumsy, half-finished paragraph, had been written in early September, whereas the blog post claimed to have been published in late October. That was promising, but he knew the committee might argue that dates on a school system could be questioned. Then, scrolling through his browser history, he noticed something he had completely forgotten: in October he had pasted an early draft into a free website called "PerfectEssay Checker" to look for grammar mistakes. A cold suspicion began to form in his mind, though he still lacked the proof to turn it into a convincing argument.

The proof came from the last person he expected. The following morning, Hamad appeared beside his locker, looking uncharacteristically uncomfortable. "Look, I owe you an apology for what I said," he muttered, avoiding Yusuf's gaze. "I was annoyed that you'd made the final and I hadn't, and I took it out on you, which was childish." Before Yusuf could respond, Hamad held up his phone. "I've been doing some digging, and that WiseWords blog has published about two hundred essays in the past year, all in completely different styles. Nobody writes like that unless they're collecting other people's work."

Sitting together in the library during their free period, the two former rivals compared the blog post with Yusuf's drafts line by line. It was Hamad who spotted it first, and he jabbed the screen so hard that the librarian glanced over disapprovingly. "Read the third sentence," he whispered. The blog described his grandfather's farm as standing "at the edge of the dessert," with the double S that turned a vast landscape of sand into a plate of pudding. Yusuf's heart skipped a beat, because he remembered that exact mistake. It had appeared in his October draft, the one he had pasted into the grammar checker, and he had corrected it himself just two days later.

That afternoon, Yusuf and Hamad laid out their evidence before Mr Kamal with the meticulous precision of lawyers presenting a case. They showed him the September draft, the October draft containing the typo, the corrected version from two days afterwards, and the blog post that had reproduced the error faithfully. They also showed him the small print of the PerfectEssay Checker website, which, buried in a paragraph nobody ever reads, granted the company the right to "store and reuse" any text users submitted. Mr Kamal stopped polishing his glasses and actually put them on, which everyone at the school knew was a remarkably good sign. "So a website stole your essay," he said slowly, "and the only reason we can prove it is that you once couldn't spell 'desert'." For the first time in a week, Yusuf laughed out loud.

The committee took less than forty-eight hours to review the evidence, and their reply was unambiguous. Yusuf had been cleared of any wrongdoing, his place in the final was fully restored, and the organisers had reported the website to the relevant authorities. More surprisingly, they asked whether he would be willing to share his experience at the awards ceremony, as a warning to other students about free online tools. On the night of the final, Yusuf did not win first prize; that went to a brilliant girl from Abha who had written about her grandmother's poetry. He came second, however, and when he walked off the stage, he found that he genuinely did not mind. His grandfather was in the front row, nodding as though the result had been entirely predictable.

A few weeks later, Hamad and Yusuf ran a workshop for the younger students called "Your Words, Your Footprints," teaching them to save every draft and to read the small print before trusting any website with their work. Hamad, who had a talent for showmanship, insisted on opening each session by projecting the infamous typo onto the screen in enormous letters. The boys always laughed, and then, quite often, they started asking thoughtful questions. Yusuf kept a printed copy of that October draft in his desk drawer, the misspelled word circled in red. Whenever he felt tempted to rush a piece of writing or take a shortcut, he would look at it and remember his grandfather's words about channels dug by hand. Mistakes, he had learned, were not always something to be ashamed of; sometimes they were the clearest evidence that the work was truly your own.

questions.q: Why was Yusuf's place in the final suspended?
options: He had missed the submission deadline.
A blog post was found that looked almost identical to his essay.
His teacher said the essay was too short.

questions.q: What does the word "relish" mean in the sentence "others seemed to relish the drama"?
options: To enjoy something greatly
To feel afraid of something
To ignore something completely

questions.q: What was the key piece of evidence that proved the blog had copied Yusuf's work?
options: A photograph of his grandfather's farm
A spelling mistake that appeared only in one of his early drafts
A message from the blog's owner admitting the theft

questions.q: What can we infer about Hamad's character from the story?
options: He is unable to admit when he is wrong.
He is jealous at first but honest and fair enough to make things right.
He secretly created the blog to harm Yusuf.

questions.q: What lesson did Yusuf and Hamad teach in their workshop?
options: How to win essay competitions easily
How to use free grammar websites more often
To save drafts and read the small print before trusting websites with their work

pages.text: The summer my grandfather finally agreed to renovate his majlis, I was the one sent to clear out the storeroom behind it, a task my older cousins had somehow wriggled out of. It smelled of dust, cardamom and decades of things nobody could bring themselves to throw away. Beneath a rolled-up carpet I found a dented tin box, its lid rusted shut, as if it had been deliberately forgotten. When I finally prised it open, I found a dozen cassette tapes, each labelled in Grandfather's careful handwriting, except one. That one bore a single word in faded blue ink, written by a stranger's hand: Muzn. I had no idea then that this small plastic rectangle would send our entire family on a journey back forty years.

I carried the box to Grandfather Hamad, who was sitting on his cushion pouring coffee with the unhurried precision of a man who had done it ten thousand times. The moment he saw the tape marked Muzn, his hand froze and a little coffee spilled onto the tray. "Where did you find that?" he asked quietly, and for once there was no teasing in his voice. I explained, half expecting to be told off for prying, but instead he simply turned the cassette over in his weathered fingers. "Some debts, Yousef, a man never manages to repay," he murmured. Then he handed it back to me and changed the subject, which, in our family, is the surest sign that a story is waiting to be told.

Nobody in our house owned a cassette player, so my sister Noura tracked one down at a second-hand market and haggled the seller down to a ridiculous price. That evening, the three of us gathered around it while the tape hissed and crackled into life. A young man's voice, nervous but sincere, filled the room. "To the truck driver called Abu Saleh," he began, "you pulled my wife and me from the flooded wadi near Al-Majma'ah, and the next night my daughter was born safe and well." He said he had named her Muzn, after the rain clouds that had nearly taken everything from him, and that he would never rest until he had thanked his rescuer in person. Grandfather sat perfectly still, but I noticed his eyes glistening in the lamplight.

Eventually, he told us the rest. In 1983, the man had posted the tape to the transport company Grandfather worked for, along with a letter containing his address. "I listened to it once in the depot and put the letter in my coat pocket, intending to reply the moment I got home," Grandfather confessed. But that same week the coat was stolen from his truck at a petrol station, and with it went the only clue to the man's identity. He had never even caught his name properly, because on that terrible night the thunder had drowned out everything. "For forty years I have wondered whether he thinks I was too proud to answer," he said, and the weight of that admission seemed to settle over the whole room.

Noura and I exchanged a glance, and I knew instantly that we were thinking the same thing. "We could find him," she said, with the kind of reckless confidence that usually gets her into trouble. Grandfather waved the idea away, insisting it was like searching for a single grain of sand in the Nafud. Nevertheless, we threw ourselves into the hunt, listening to the tape over and over for anything that might narrow it down. In the background of the recording, we eventually picked out a muffled announcement mentioning a school in Unaizah. It was a slender thread, but it was the only one we had, and we clung to it.

Over the following week, we contacted heritage groups, local historians and anyone in Unaizah who might be willing to answer a polite message from two teenagers in Riyadh. Most people were kind but unhelpful, and a few clearly suspected we were up to something. One elderly gentleman spent forty minutes on the phone recounting the floods of the early eighties without ever getting to the point. By Thursday, even Noura's enthusiasm had begun to wane, and I was on the verge of admitting that Grandfather had been right all along. Then, almost as an afterthought, Mother asked a question that turned everything on its head. "Have you tried looking for the daughter instead?" she said. "A woman named Muzn, born in the spring of 1983, would be about forty now."

It was so obvious that I felt slightly foolish for having overlooked it. Noura searched school websites and community pages and, within an hour, came across a deputy headteacher in Unaizah called Muzn whose biography mentioned that she had been born during a famous storm. With Mother's permission and her help in drafting a respectful message, we wrote to the school explaining everything. The reply arrived the next morning, and Noura read it aloud with trembling hands. "My father has spoken about Abu Saleh my entire life," Muzn had written. "He is eighty-one now, and he has never stopped hoping."

Two weeks later, a dusty white car pulled up outside our house, and an old man in a brown bisht stepped out, leaning on the arm of his son. Grandfather was waiting at the door, dressed in his best thobe, looking more nervous than I had ever seen him. For a long moment the two men simply stared at each other, as though trying to recognise the young faces hidden beneath the years. Then Uncle Mansour, as we would soon be calling him, opened his arms, and Grandfather embraced him like a brother returned from a long journey. Meanwhile, Muzn and her mother were welcomed by my mother and grandmother in the family sitting room, where, judging by the sounds drifting through the wall, there was just as much laughter and just as many tears.

In the majlis, over dates and endless cups of coffee, the truth finally came out on both sides. Uncle Mansour admitted that when no reply came, he had assumed his tape had been lost, never once imagining that his rescuer had been carrying guilt of his own. "You owe me nothing, Abu Saleh," he insisted, gesturing towards his son and grandsons. "Everything I have, I have because you stopped your truck that night when everyone else drove past." Grandfather shook his head and replied that a man who stops to help is only doing what Allah expects of him. I sat in the corner, pouring coffee and trying not to stare, realising that I was watching a forty-year silence finally come to an end.

That night, after our guests had gone, Grandfather asked me to fetch the old cassette player and a blank tape. "It is long overdue," he said with a rare, mischievous smile, "but a reply is still a reply." He spoke into the machine for nearly half an hour, telling Uncle Mansour about the storm, the stolen coat and the decades of wondering. When he had finished, he labelled the cassette himself and handed it to me to post first thing in the morning. On the label, in his careful handwriting, he had written two words: For Muzn. I understood then that family is not only the people we are born to, but also the people we refuse to forget.

questions.q: Why did Grandfather Hamad never reply to the man on the tape?
options: The letter with the address was stolen along with his coat
He was too proud to accept thanks
He did not understand the message on the tape

questions.q: Why did the man name his daughter Muzn?
options: It was his mother's name
It referred to the rain clouds from the night of the flood
It was the name of the school in Unaizah

questions.q: In the story, what does the word 'wane' mean in 'even Noura's enthusiasm had begun to wane'?
options: To grow stronger
To become weaker
To change direction

questions.q: What can we infer about Grandfather's feelings over the forty years?
options: He had completely forgotten the rescue
He was angry that Mansour never contacted him
He felt guilty that Mansour might think he was ungrateful or proud

questions.q: Whose idea finally led Yousef and Noura to the right family?
options: Their mother's suggestion to search for the daughter
An elderly historian on the phone
Grandfather's memory of Mansour's name

stories.title: The Light in the Locked Room

pages.text: In the year 1011, the book market of Cairo was a maze of ink, dust and argument, and fifteen-year-old Yusuf knew every corner of it. He was an apprentice to an elderly copyist, and his days were spent carrying freshly written manuscripts to scholars who paid well and complained even better. His favourite customer was a quiet man from Basra named al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham, who read faster than anyone Yusuf had ever met and never once haggled over the price. One morning, however, Yusuf arrived at the scholar's door to find him pacing the room like a caged lion. "I have done something foolish," Ibn al-Haytham admitted, without even glancing at the books. "Back in Basra, I once made a careless boast that the floods of the Nile could be controlled by human hands, and somehow the words have reached the ears of the Caliph himself."

The Caliph al-Hakim was a ruler whose moods could change as suddenly as desert weather, and a summons from his palace was not something any sensible man ignored. Within a week, Ibn al-Haytham had been given money, workers and a clear command: travel south and tame the great river. To Yusuf's astonishment, the scholar asked for him by name. "You have sharp eyes and a sharper memory," he said, "and I shall need someone to write down everything we see." Yusuf's master grumbled about losing his best apprentice, but nobody refused the Caliph's guest. So it was that a boy who had never left the city found himself on a boat drifting south, with the green fields of Egypt sliding past on either side.

After weeks of travel, they reached Aswan, where the Nile tumbled over a wild stretch of rocks known as the cataract. Ibn al-Haytham stood on the bank for hours, measuring, sketching and saying almost nothing. Along the river rose temples built by ancient kings, their stone columns so enormous that Yusuf felt like an ant beside them. "Look carefully at these monuments," the scholar said at last, his voice heavy. "The people who built them understood geometry and engineering better than we give them credit for, and they had thousands of labourers at their command." He paused, watching the water roar between the rocks. "If they could have controlled this river, they would have done so long ago."

That night, they sat beside a small fire while the river murmured in the darkness. "So the task is impossible," Yusuf said quietly, hardly daring to say the words aloud. "With the tools we possess, yes," Ibn al-Haytham replied, "and now I must return to Cairo and tell the most unpredictable ruler in the world that I cannot keep my promise." Yusuf had heard the stories that whispered through the markets: officials who had fallen from favour overnight, and others who had simply disappeared. "Couldn't you pretend the work is progressing, just to buy some time?" he suggested. The scholar shook his head firmly. "A lie built on a river is still a lie, and sooner or later the water washes it away."

What happened next took Yusuf completely by surprise. A few days after their return, Ibn al-Haytham appeared in the street with his turban crooked, muttering nonsense and laughing at nothing at all. Rumours spread like wildfire: the brilliant scholar from Basra had lost his mind. Yusuf rushed to his house, terrified, only to receive a calm, knowing look the moment the door was shut. "Lower your voice," the scholar whispered. "A ruler cannot punish a madman for failing at his task, but he can certainly punish a sane one." Within the week, the Caliph's officers had confiscated his property and placed him under guard, and Yusuf realised that his friend had feigned madness to save his life, at the cost of his freedom.

His confinement took place in a small house near the great mosque of al-Azhar, and Yusuf, being young and harmless-looking, was permitted to bring food each day. The room was gloomy, for the wooden shutters were kept tightly closed against the scorching afternoon sun. One afternoon, as Yusuf set down a bowl of lentils, he noticed something extraordinary on the whitewashed wall. A tiny crack in the shutters was letting in a thin beam of light, and on the wall glowed a faint, coloured picture of the street outside, with its passers-by walking along, every one of them upside down. Yusuf stared, half expecting it to vanish. Behind him, Ibn al-Haytham was smiling for the first time in months. "I have been watching that little miracle all week," he said, "and I believe it is going to keep me busy for years."

From then on, the locked room became a laboratory hidden in plain sight. Yusuf smuggled in candles, scraps of paper and lengths of string, and together they tested how light behaved when it passed through holes of different sizes. They lit three candles in a row and watched three separate points of light appear on the wall, each travelling in its own perfectly straight line. For centuries, many respected thinkers had believed that the eye sent out invisible rays to touch the objects it saw, but the experiments pointed firmly in the opposite direction. "Light comes from the object and enters the eye," Ibn al-Haytham declared, tapping his notes. "It is not enough to trust the great books, Yusuf; we must test every idea, record every result, and be prepared to overturn even the opinions of giants."

Their secret, however, was always hanging by a thread. One evening, a new guard pressed his ear to the door and heard what was unmistakably a reasoned conversation about angles and reflection. He burst in, eyes narrowed, demanding to know why a supposed madman was speaking like a teacher at a college. Yusuf's heart was pounding, but he forced himself to laugh. "Sir, he has been explaining to me for an hour that the moon is a polished copper plate hanging from the ceiling!" On cue, Ibn al-Haytham leapt up and began bowing deeply to a candle, addressing it as "Your Majesty", and the guard backed out, shaking his head in pity. Only when his footsteps had faded did the two of them dare to breathe again.

The months turned into years, and the boy who had once carried manuscripts grew into a young man with ink permanently staining his fingers. Then, in 1021, astonishing news swept through Cairo: the Caliph had ridden out alone one night into the Muqattam hills and had never returned. Nobody knew what had become of him, and his mysterious disappearance would be debated for centuries. Within days, Ibn al-Haytham's "madness" had made a remarkably speedy recovery, and his property was quietly returned to him. Standing in the open street for the first time in a decade, he shielded his eyes against the dazzling sunlight. "Ten years of darkness," he said thoughtfully, "and yet I have never seen so clearly."

What he produced from those lost years was the Book of Optics, a treatise in seven volumes that patiently explained vision, reflection and the bending of light, and Yusuf copied every page with pride. Long after his master had passed away, the work was translated into Latin and studied in Europe, where it shaped the thinking of scientists for hundreds of years. Its insistence on careful testing rather than blind trust helped to lay the foundations of the scientific method that researchers still rely on today. When Yusuf was an old man, his grandson once asked him what the most important thing he had learned from the great scholar was. Yusuf did not answer at once; instead, he closed the shutters, pierced a tiny hole with a needle, and waited. As the courtyard appeared, glowing and upside down, on the wall, the boy gasped, and Yusuf smiled. "Courage is not only facing danger," he said softly. "Sometimes it is having the humility to admit what you cannot do, and the perseverance to discover what you can."

pages.text: The old stone house in Abha had stood empty for almost a decade, and by the time Lina pushed open its heavy wooden door, the smell of dust and damp rushed out to greet her like an impatient relative. Her uncle Mansour was already inside, clipboard in hand, measuring cracks with the grim satisfaction of a man who had been proved right. "The roof leaks, the walls are crumbling, and the electrics are older than your father," he announced, without looking up. "The builders start on Thursday, and frankly, not a moment too soon." Lina barely heard him, because her eyes had drifted to the far wall of the majlis. Even beneath a veil of grime, it blazed with colour: bands of crimson, ochre and deep green, triangles nested inside diamonds, lines of white dots marching across the plaster like tiny soldiers. She had seen photographs of Al-Qatt Al-Asiri in school, but standing in front of the real thing, painted by her own great-grandmother Hessa, took her breath away.

As she stepped closer, Lina noticed something odd about the pattern. Every panel was crowded with shapes and colour, except one in the lower right corner, which had been left almost entirely bare. Squinting, she could just make out faint charcoal lines sketched across it, as though someone had planned a design and then simply walked away. "Uncle, what happens to this wall?" she asked, trying to keep her voice casual. Mansour finally glanced up, and his expression softened for a moment before hardening again. "It's beautiful, I know, but the plaster is coming away in places, and damp is getting in behind it. We'll have to cover it with fresh cement, or the whole room will rot."

The following afternoon, a sleek car pulled up outside, and a man in a crisp white thobe introduced himself as Mr. Kassab, the owner of a gallery in Jeddah. He walked along the painted wall slowly, nodding as if he were doing sums in his head, which, Lina suspected, he was. "Collectors would pay a great deal for authentic panels like these," he said smoothly. "My team can cut them out in sections, frame them, and sell them on your behalf, and the money would more than cover your repairs." Uncle Mansour rubbed his chin, clearly tempted, and Lina felt her stomach drop. The thought of her great-grandmother's work hanging in pieces in strangers' homes, separated like the pages of a torn book, struck her as nothing short of a betrayal. "Give me until Thursday," Mansour said at last, and Mr. Kassab smiled the patient smile of someone who rarely lost a deal.

That evening, Lina persuaded her older brother Faris to walk with her to the house of Umm Saeed, an elderly neighbour who, according to family legend, had painted walls all over the village in her youth. They found her on her terrace, wrapped in a shawl, pouring cardamom coffee into tiny cups. When Lina described the bare panel, the old woman set down the pot and laughed softly, her eyes glistening. "So she never told any of you," she murmured. "Hessa and I painted that majlis together, the year your grandfather was born, and she refused to let me fill that corner." Lina leaned forward, hardly daring to breathe.

"In those days, the women of the house painted the walls before every Eid and every wedding," Umm Saeed explained, tracing a triangle in the air with one wrinkled finger. "Hessa used to say that a wall is never truly finished while a family still lives behind it. She left that space for whoever came next, a daughter, a granddaughter, anyone with the patience to learn." Faris raised his eyebrows at his sister, who had gone very quiet. "And the charcoal lines?" Lina asked eventually. "Just a suggestion," the old woman replied, with a mischievous shrug. "She always said the next painter should feel free to ignore her completely."

Umm Saeed's expression darkened, however, when Lina mentioned Mr. Kassab's offer. "Cut them out?" she repeated, horrified. "These walls are mud and stone, child, not canvas; the moment a saw touches them, the plaster will shatter like glass." Lina's mind began racing, and by the time she and Faris got home, she had already drawn up a plan. She spent half the night reading articles on heritage conservation, watching interviews with restorers, and taking careful photographs of every crack in the majlis. She even discovered that Al-Qatt Al-Asiri had been recognised by UNESCO as part of humanity's cultural heritage, which made the idea of selling it off in chunks seem even more absurd. By dawn, her eyes were bloodshot, but she had a proposal that, she hoped, even her practical uncle couldn't dismiss out of hand.

Rather than wait for permission, Lina decided to prove the wall could be saved. For three nights, Umm Saeed taught her how to clean the old paint with nothing harsher than soft brushes and patience, and how to mix colours the way they had once been mixed, though nowadays they used modern pigments alongside the traditional ones. Faris, who claimed to have no artistic talent whatsoever, held the lamp and offered unhelpful commentary, yet never once suggested going to bed. Lina made countless mistakes: a line that wobbled, a green that dried far too dark, a dot that turned stubbornly into a smudge. Each time, Umm Saeed simply handed her a damp cloth and said, "Again." Slowly, as the grime lifted, the old colours began to glow, and the wall seemed to wake from a very long sleep.

On Thursday morning, Mr. Kassab arrived with two workmen and an electric saw, and Uncle Mansour followed them into the majlis, looking tired and resigned. He stopped dead in the doorway. One whole section of the wall, freshly cleaned, now shone as brilliantly as it must have done seventy years earlier, and in its centre, previously hidden beneath dirt, a delicate pattern of interlocking lines spelled out a single name: Hessa. "She signed it," Mansour whispered, his clipboard hanging forgotten at his side. Lina stepped forward and, with a voice steadier than she felt, explained what Umm Saeed had told her about the fragile plaster, showing him photographs, articles and a rough estimate she had made of what it would actually cost to repair the leaking roof. Mr. Kassab cleared his throat impatiently, but nobody was paying him the slightest attention.

For a long moment, Uncle Mansour said nothing at all. Then he turned to the gallery owner and, with impeccable politeness, thanked him for his time and showed him to the door. "I've been so focused on what this house was costing us," he admitted afterwards, "that I completely lost sight of what it's worth." Within days, the whole family had rolled up their sleeves: cousins carried tiles up ladders, Faris discovered a surprising talent for fixing gutters, and a conservation specialist from the regional heritage office came to advise on sealing the damp. The builders still came, but this time they repaired the roof instead of plastering over the past. Umm Saeed supervised everything from a plastic chair in the courtyard, issuing instructions like a general commanding her troops.

On the eve of Eid, with the house full of relatives and the scent of incense drifting through the rooms, Lina finally knelt before the empty corner of the wall. She had studied Hessa's charcoal lines for weeks, and in the end she kept some and boldly ignored others, just as her great-grandmother had invited her to. She painted a band of the deep green Hessa had loved, framed it with crimson triangles, and, at its heart, wove her own name into the pattern so subtly that only someone who knew where to look would ever find it. When she stepped back, the room fell silent, and then Umm Saeed began to clap, and soon everyone had joined in. Yet Lina had done one more thing that nobody noticed until much later: in the very corner of her panel, she had left a small space untouched. After all, she thought with a smile, a wall is never truly finished while a family still lives behind it.

options: She plans to continue Hessa's tradition for future generations
She forgot to finish her painting
She wants Mr. Kassab to buy that part later

pages.text: Huda had made up her mind, long before the car turned into the narrow lanes of Al-Balad, that this was going to be the dullest weekend of her life. Her family had spent months restoring Bayt al-Nour, the crumbling coral-stone house in old Jeddah where her grandmother had grown up, and every visit seemed to involve dust, heat and endless conversations about wooden beams. "You could at least pretend to be interested," her older brother muttered as they climbed out into the humid afternoon. Huda rolled her eyes, though she couldn't help glancing up at the enormous wooden roshan that jutted out from the first floor, its lattice of interlocking stars throwing delicate shadows onto the street. She had walked past that window a hundred times without really looking at it. Her grandmother, leaning on her stick in the doorway, smiled as if she knew something Huda didn't.

"I need someone with young eyes to sort out the storeroom on the top floor," her grandmother announced, and before Huda could come up with an excuse, she found herself climbing a staircase that creaked in protest at every step. The storeroom was crammed with chests, rolled-up carpets and boxes that hadn't been opened for decades. Wedged behind a cracked mirror, she discovered a bundle wrapped in faded green cloth. Inside lay a brass astrolabe, its surface engraved with tiny Arabic letters and the names of stars, together with a scrap of paper on which someone had written in careful handwriting: "Turn it only towards the evening star, and return before it sets." Huda assumed it was some kind of family joke, yet her fingers were trembling slightly as she rotated the delicate inner disc. The moment the pointer settled on the star marked Al-Zuhara, a warm wind that smelled unmistakably of salt swept through the windowless room.

When the dizziness faded, the first thing Huda noticed was the silence where the hum of air conditioners should have been. She was standing in the same storeroom, but it was almost empty, and through a gap in the shutters she could see the masts of wooden dhows rocking in a harbour that seemed impossibly close. Somewhere below, the call to prayer drifted over rooftops that had no satellite dishes, and a man was leading a heavily loaded camel through the lane. "Who are you, and what on earth are you wearing?" demanded a voice behind her. Huda spun round to face a girl of about her own age, dressed in a long embroidered dress, clutching a battered notebook to her chest. Thinking on her feet, Huda claimed she was a cousin visiting from Makkah, and to her astonishment, the girl, whose name was Fatimah, seemed to accept the story without a second thought.

It didn't take long for Huda to work out that she had landed somewhere in the 1940s, nor to realise, with a jolt, that Fatimah's family name was the same as her own. Over glasses of sweet mint tea in the courtyard, Fatimah explained that her father, a carpenter, had been commissioned to build a new roshan for the front of the house. "I've been designing patterns for it for months," she confided, opening her notebook to reveal pages covered in intricate geometric sketches. "But the master carpenter says a girl's drawings belong in the kitchen fire, and my father won't go against him unless the design is perfect." She traced the central motif with her finger, an elaborate star that simply refused to close properly at its edges. "If I can't solve it by tomorrow morning, I'm going to give up for good."

Huda stared at the half-finished pattern, and a shiver ran down her spine, because she had seen it only hours earlier, carved in wood above the street. The star that Fatimah couldn't complete was the very one in the window she had dismissed as old-fashioned on her way in. "The problem isn't your idea," she said slowly, "it's the angles; you're trying to fit eight points into a circle without dividing it evenly first." She borrowed a piece of string and a nail, and, drawing on a geometry lesson she had barely paid attention to the previous term, showed Fatimah how to construct perfect divisions using nothing but a fixed point and a steady hand. Fatimah's eyes widened as the lines began to fall into place, each one locking neatly into the next like pieces of a puzzle. For the first time in her life, Huda understood that maths could be beautiful.

They worked late into the evening by the flickering light of an oil lamp, arguing cheerfully over curves and spacing, and laughing whenever the ink smudged. Every so often, Huda glanced anxiously at the astrolabe hidden in the folds of her abaya, where the pointer was creeping steadily towards the horizon line. She had no idea what would happen if the evening star set while she was still here, and she certainly didn't intend to find out the hard way. Yet she couldn't bring herself to leave before the design was finished, not when Fatimah was humming happily beside her, more confident with every stroke of the pen. "You've got a gift for this, you know," Huda said quietly, and she meant every word. Fatimah looked up, startled, as though nobody had ever told her so before.

Just as the last line was drawn, Fatimah's father stepped into the courtyard, wiping sawdust from his hands. He studied the drawing for a long time without speaking, while both girls held their breath. "Who taught you to divide the circle like this?" he finally asked his daughter, and Fatimah, after a quick glance at Huda, answered that a friend had shown her the method, but the pattern itself was entirely her own. Her father nodded slowly, a smile tugging at the corners of his mouth. "Then the master carpenter will have to eat his words, because this is the design we'll use," he declared. Fatimah let out a cry of delight, and in the excitement nobody noticed Huda slipping quietly up the stairs.

At the top of the staircase, Fatimah caught up with her, breathless and puzzled. "You're not really from Makkah, are you?" she asked, and Huda, unable to lie to her a second time, simply shook her head. Fatimah considered this for a moment, then pressed something into her hand: a small pencil sketch of the finished star, signed with her name in neat, determined letters. "Wherever you're going, take this so you don't forget me," she said. Huda swallowed the lump in her throat and promised that she never would. Then, with the evening star trembling on the very edge of the horizon, she turned the brass disc back to where it had started.

She found herself sprawled on the dusty floor of the crowded storeroom, with the noise of traffic and air conditioners rushing back into her ears. According to her phone, barely a minute had passed, yet the sketch was still clutched tightly in her fist, the paper yellow and brittle with age. Huda hurried downstairs and out into the street, where she stood gazing up at the roshan as though seeing it for the first time. Every line of the star was exactly as she and Fatimah had drawn it by lamplight. "Your great-grandmother designed that, you know," her grandmother said, appearing beside her. "She used to tell us that a mysterious guest helped her finish it, a girl with the strangest shoes anyone had ever seen."

Huda looked down at her trainers and burst out laughing, while her grandmother raised a curious eyebrow but, wisely, asked no questions. For the rest of the weekend, nobody could drag her away from the restoration work, and her brother joked that she had been replaced by an entirely different person. In a sense, she supposed, she had. That evening she carefully placed the sketch inside a frame and hung it in the room where she and Fatimah had worked together, decades apart and yet side by side. Before she fell asleep, she opened a new notebook and wrote on the first page, in neat and determined letters: "Future architect." Somewhere, she felt sure, a girl in an embroidered dress would have approved.

pages.text: Faisal had always considered his grandfather's stories charming but hopelessly out of date, like a cassette tape in a world of streaming. So when Jaddi Saad announced, over Friday lunch, that he intended to find the old well where his own father had once watered camels, Faisal barely looked up from his phone. 'Nobody navigates by memory anymore, Jaddi,' he said, with the easy confidence of a sixteen-year-old who had never been truly lost. His sister Noura, who was a year older and never went anywhere without her camera, kicked him under the table. Their grandfather merely smiled and unfolded a piece of yellowed paper covered in faded ink. 'This map has no roads on it,' he said quietly, 'because when it was drawn, there were none.'

They set off before dawn three days later, the old Land Cruiser loaded with water, dates and enough blankets to survive a winter on a mountaintop. The red dunes of the Nafud rose around them like frozen waves, their crests glowing as the sun crept over the horizon. Faisal had the route saved on a GPS device, which he consulted every few minutes with obvious satisfaction. Jaddi Saad, by contrast, kept glancing at the sky and at the shapes of distant rocks, as though reading a book that only he could see. On the hand-drawn map, the well was marked by a small circle beside a sketch of a rock shaped like a camel's head. 'If the sand hasn't swallowed it,' their grandfather murmured, 'we'll be drinking from it by sunset.'

The storm came out of nowhere, or at least that was how it seemed to Faisal. One moment the sky was a flawless blue; the next, a brown wall was rolling towards them, devouring the dunes one by one. Jaddi Saad pulled over at once, turned the car away from the wind and told them to cover their faces. For almost an hour, sand hissed against the windows like rain made of glass, and the world shrank to the inside of the vehicle. When the wind finally died down, the Land Cruiser was buried up to its wheels, the GPS screen had gone completely black, and Faisal's phone showed not a single bar of signal. Worse still, one of the water containers had split open where a loose toolbox had crashed into it.

Digging the car out proved to be harder than any of them had anticipated. Halfway through, Jaddi Saad stepped awkwardly into a hollow in the sand, and his ankle twisted beneath him with a sickening crack. Noura wrapped it tightly with a scarf while Faisal tried, and failed, to hide his panic. They took stock of their situation: one remaining container of water, an injured grandfather, and a car that was going nowhere. 'Normally, the golden rule is to stay with the vehicle,' Jaddi Saad said, his face pale but calm. 'But with this little water, waiting could cost us dearly, and the well is no more than fifteen kilometres to the east, where herders camp at this time of year.'

It was decided that Noura would stay with their grandfather in the shade of the car, while Faisal would walk to the well once the sun had set and the heat had eased. As darkness fell, Jaddi Saad pointed to a faint, steady star low in the northern sky. 'That is Al-Jadi,' he said. 'Every other star circles around it, but it never moves, which is why travellers have trusted it for a thousand years.' He explained that if Faisal kept Al-Jadi over his left shoulder, he would be heading east, towards the rock shaped like a camel's head. Faisal repeated the instructions until he could have recited them in his sleep. For the first time in his life, he found himself hanging on his grandfather's every word.

The desert at night was nothing like Faisal had imagined. The silence was so complete that he could hear his own heartbeat, and every shadow seemed to shift when he wasn't looking. More than once, he became convinced that he had drifted off course, and each time he forced himself to stop, breathe, and find Al-Jadi again. Had he been alone with only his own thoughts, he might well have given up. Instead, he kept hearing his grandfather's voice: 'Don't argue with the sky, Faisal; it has been right far longer than you have.' Hour after hour, he trudged over dunes that all looked identical, sipping his water sparingly and counting his steps to keep his mind from wandering.

By the time the eastern sky began to turn pink, Faisal's legs were trembling with exhaustion. Then, as the light grew stronger, he saw it: a dark outcrop of rock with a long neck and a blunt nose, unmistakably the camel's head from the map. A wave of relief swept over him, only to be replaced by dismay, because there was no sign of any well. He circled the rock twice, his heart sinking further with every step. It was then that he noticed fresh camel tracks pressed into the sand, all heading in the same direction around a low ridge. Mustering his last reserves of energy, he followed them.

Beyond the ridge lay a stone-lined well, a cluster of tents and a herd of camels drinking noisily from a trough. An elderly man in a brown cloak looked up in astonishment as Faisal stumbled towards him, dusty and barely able to speak. Within minutes, Faisal was sitting on a rug with a cup of water in one hand and a glass of sweet tea in the other. When he mentioned his grandfather's name, the old man's eyes widened. 'Saad bin Mansour? We were boys together at this very well, more than sixty years ago!' he exclaimed. Before Faisal had even finished his tea, the man's sons were loading a pickup truck with water and a first-aid kit.

They found the Land Cruiser easily, partly because Noura had been flashing sunlight towards the horizon with her makeup mirror ever since dawn. Jaddi Saad was weary and his ankle had swollen badly, but his spirits were remarkably high. When he saw his childhood friend climbing out of the truck, he laughed so hard that he had to wipe tears from his eyes. Noura threw her arms around her brother, scolding him and thanking him in the same breath. Faisal, for his part, couldn't stop grinning, though he was too tired to say much at all. Later that afternoon, Noura took a photograph of the two old men sitting side by side, which would end up framed on the wall of their family majlis.

A week later, with his grandfather's ankle in a cast, Faisal knocked on his door holding a fresh sheet of paper and a pen. 'I'd like to make a copy of your map,' he said, a little sheepishly, 'and I was hoping you could teach me the rest of the stars.' Jaddi Saad raised an eyebrow, clearly enjoying the moment, before patting the cushion beside him. Together they redrew the dunes, the camel's head rock and the well, and in the corner Faisal added a tiny star labelled Al-Jadi. His phone lay forgotten on the table, buzzing with messages he would answer later. Some maps, Faisal had come to realise, show you where to go, while others show you who you are.

pages.text: The fog rolled over the Sarawat Mountains like a living thing, swallowing the road ahead until Faisal could barely make out the edge of the cliff. His uncle Tariq drove with one hand on the wheel, apparently untroubled by the thousand-metre drop just beyond the window. ‘You’ll get used to it,’ he said, glancing at his nephew’s white knuckles. ‘By the end of the summer, you’ll be driving this road in your dreams.’ Faisal doubted it, but he kept his thoughts to himself. He had agreed to spend six weeks at his uncle’s wildlife research station largely because his parents had insisted, and partly because anything seemed better than another summer of staring at his phone in the Riyadh heat. Now, as the jagged peaks emerged from the mist, he began to suspect that he had underestimated this place.

The research station turned out to be little more than two stone buildings, a water tank and a room crammed with computers. On the very first morning, Uncle Tariq handed him a hard drive and a cup of cardamom coffee. ‘Your job,’ he explained, ‘is to go through the footage from our camera traps and log every animal you see.’ The cameras, strapped to trees and rocks across the valley, were triggered by movement, which meant that Faisal spent hours watching foxes sniffing at the lens, hyraxes sunbathing and troops of baboons squabbling over nothing in particular. ‘What exactly are we looking for?’ he asked on the third day, rubbing his tired eyes. His uncle paused, and when he answered, his voice was almost reverent: ‘The Arabian leopard. There may be fewer than two hundred left in the wild, and nobody has photographed one in this valley for eleven years.’

Faisal was beginning to think the leopard was little more than a legend when the phone rang early one morning. Uncle Tariq listened in silence, his expression darkening with every second. Four goats belonging to Abu Saleh, an elderly herder in the village below, had been found dead in their enclosure at dawn. ‘People are saying it was the leopard,’ his uncle said grimly as he hung up. ‘Some of the younger men are already talking about setting traps.’ Faisal felt a strange twist in his stomach, as though something he had only just begun to care about was already slipping out of reach. Within ten minutes, they were bouncing down the mountain track, the sun burning away the last of the mist.

Abu Saleh was a tall, weathered man whose family had herded goats on these slopes for generations. He received them with the courtesy that tradition demanded, pouring coffee and offering dates, but there was no mistaking the anger simmering beneath his calm. ‘My grandfather spoke of the leopard with respect,’ he said, ‘but respect does not feed my family.’ Several men stood nearby, arms folded, clearly unconvinced by the scientist from the city. Uncle Tariq did not argue; instead, he chose his words with great care. ‘Give us three days,’ he said. ‘If we cannot prove what did this, I will personally help you protect your animals, whatever it takes.’ After a long, uncomfortable silence, the old man nodded once.

While the adults talked, Faisal wandered over to the enclosure, where the ground was soft from recent rain. He crouched down and studied a confusion of prints pressed into the mud, remembering something his uncle had mentioned during one of their long evenings at the station. Cats, including leopards, retract their claws when they walk, so their tracks show only rounded pads; dogs, on the other hand, leave the sharp marks of their claws behind. Faisal took out his phone, placed a pen beside the clearest print for scale, and photographed it from several angles. The tiny triangular marks at the front of each toe were unmistakable. ‘Uncle,’ he called, trying to keep the excitement out of his voice, ‘I think you should take a look at this.’

The tracks were promising, but Uncle Tariq warned that a few photographs in the mud would hardly change anyone’s mind. ‘People believe what they see with their own eyes,’ he said. So that evening, armed with a thermal camera borrowed from the station, Faisal settled into a hiding place behind a low stone wall overlooking the enclosure. To his surprise, he was not alone for long: Abu Saleh’s grandson Hamad, a quiet boy of about his own age, climbed up beside him carrying a flask of tea. ‘My grandfather wants to know the truth as much as you do,’ Hamad murmured, handing him a cup. The hours crept by, and the two boys spoke in whispers about school, football and the strange silence of the mountains after dark. Somewhere in the valley, an owl called, and then the night went utterly still.

It was just after two o’clock when Hamad gripped Faisal’s arm. On the grey screen of the thermal camera, five glowing shapes were slinking down the slope towards the goats, low and purposeful. They were not cats; their ears were pointed, their tails swung loosely, and they moved together in a tight, practised group. ‘Feral dogs,’ Faisal breathed, his heart hammering against his ribs. He kept the camera steady while Hamad switched on a powerful torch and shouted at the top of his lungs. The pack scattered instantly, vanishing into the darkness with frightened yelps, and inside the enclosure the goats bleated in panic but remained unharmed. For a moment, the two boys simply stared at each other, hardly able to believe what they had witnessed.

The next afternoon, half the village crowded into Abu Saleh’s majlis to watch the footage on Faisal’s laptop. Nobody spoke as the ghostly figures of the dogs crept across the screen, and when the clip ended, a murmur of astonishment rippled through the room. Abu Saleh turned to Faisal and studied him for a long moment. ‘It seems we nearly punished an innocent creature for another’s crime,’ he admitted. ‘That would have been a great injustice, and a great shame.’ Uncle Tariq then explained that the station would help the village build stronger enclosures and work with local authorities to deal with the dog pack humanely. By the time the coffee had been served for a third time, the talk of traps had died away completely.

On his final morning, Faisal hiked up to retrieve the memory card from the most remote camera, perched high on a ridge that he had never visited before. Back at the station, he loaded the files without much expectation, half-listening to his uncle making breakfast in the next room. Then he froze. In the pale light of dawn, a female leopard was walking along the ridge, her spotted coat almost invisible against the rocks, her eyes glowing gold. Behind her, stumbling clumsily over a stone, came a single tiny cub. ‘Uncle Tariq!’ he shouted, so loudly that a cup crashed to the floor. His uncle rushed in, stared at the screen, and for the first time that summer, Faisal saw a grown man completely lost for words.

Before they left the mountains, they drove down to the village one last time to show Abu Saleh the photograph. The old man held the printed picture in his hands for a long while, tracing the outline of the cub with one rough finger. ‘My grandfather would have been happy to see this,’ he said quietly. ‘Tell me, young man, what will you do with your life now?’ Faisal hesitated, then realised that the answer had been forming inside him all summer without his noticing. ‘I think I’d like to come back,’ he said, ‘and help make sure there are still leopards here when Hamad’s grandchildren are old enough to look for them.’ As they climbed the winding road out of the valley, the fog rolled in once more, and this time Faisal did not grip the seat at all.

pages.text: Yusuf had always thought of his grandfather's house in Al-Balad as a ship that had somehow run aground in the middle of Jeddah. Its walls were built of coral stone dragged from the Red Sea a century and a half ago, and its tall wooden roshan windows leaned out over the narrow lane like curious faces. This week, however, the old house felt less like a ship and more like a museum waiting to happen. On Thursday morning, a curator from the new heritage centre was coming to collect the family's most precious possession: the pearl ledger kept by Yusuf's great-great-grandfather, a merchant who had traded with India and the Gulf. Every page recorded a voyage, a price, a name, and occasionally a storm that had nearly cost a crew their lives. Yusuf, who was sixteen and secretly proud of the whole thing, had been counting down the days.

On Tuesday morning, the ledger was gone. Yusuf's father discovered the empty space on the study desk just after Fajr, and within minutes the entire household had gathered in the doorway, speaking over one another. "It can't simply have walked away," said Uncle Faisal, running a hand over his beard. "Someone has taken it, and I don't think we need to look very far." Every head turned, almost against its will, towards the courtyard, where Hamid the carpenter was already unpacking his tools. For three weeks he had been restoring the study's roshan, carefully replacing panels that termites had hollowed out over the decades. He was the only outsider who had spent any time in that room.

Yusuf felt a knot tighten in his stomach as he watched Hamid's face change when he realised what was being implied. The carpenter put down his chisel, walked calmly to the doorway and offered to empty every bag and box he owned. "I have worked in this neighbourhood for thirty years," he said quietly, "and no family has ever had reason to count their spoons after I left." Uncle Faisal muttered something about formalities, but the damage had clearly been done. Later, Yusuf's younger sister Lina pulled him aside with the sharp expression she wore when a maths problem refused to behave. "Here's what bothers me," she whispered. "The study was locked last night, and the only key hangs on Jiddo's chain, which he never takes off."

That afternoon, while the adults argued politely in the majlis, Yusuf let himself into the study to look for himself. There was no sign of forced entry: the lock was undamaged, and Hamid's new roshan panels were firmly fixed and still smelled of fresh cedar. On the desk, a thin film of dust had settled everywhere except for a clean rectangle where the ledger had rested for years. Then he noticed something on the floor that he had walked past a hundred times without seeing. A faint trail of fine sawdust, carried from Hamid's workbench, led from the desk towards the door, pressed into the shape of footprints. They were not the marks of work boots, but of soft slippers, one of them worn noticeably flat at the heel, the way a man wears them when he drags his left foot slightly.

Yusuf knew only one person in the house who walked like that. His grandfather was eighty-seven, and over the past year his memory had begun to drift in and out like the tide, sharp one hour and clouded the next. At dinner that evening, Jiddo stared into his cup of cardamom coffee for a long time before speaking. "The water came up to the third step," he murmured, to nobody in particular. "You must keep the book dry." Uncle Faisal patted his arm gently and changed the subject, assuming the old man was lost in some distant afternoon. Yusuf, however, could not shake the feeling that his grandfather had just told them exactly where to look, if only they knew how to listen.

After dinner, Lina found Yusuf sitting on the staircase, turning the words over in his mind. "Don't you remember the story he used to tell us when we were little?" she asked, settling beside him. "The year of the great rain, when he was a boy, and the lane outside turned into a river overnight." Gradually it came back to Yusuf: how the floodwater had crept into the house, how young Jiddo had been terrified that the family's papers would be ruined, and how he had hidden something precious until the danger passed. In those days, of course, nobody had dreamed of museums; the ledger had simply been the record of how the family earned its bread. Yusuf looked down at the worn steps beneath him and felt the hairs on his arms rise.

They decided to wait until the house was asleep, partly out of curiosity and partly because neither of them wanted to raise false hopes. Shortly after midnight, a soft shuffling sound drifted down the corridor, and the two of them pressed themselves into the shadow of the stairwell. Their grandfather appeared, wrapped in his shawl, moving slowly but with surprising purpose. He paused at the bottom of the staircase, counted under his breath, and laid his palm flat against the wall beside the third step, as though reassuring himself that something was still there. Outside, rain was pattering against the roshan, an unusual sound in Jeddah, and Yusuf suddenly understood what had woken the old man's memory two nights earlier. Satisfied, Jiddo turned and shuffled back to bed without noticing his grandchildren holding their breath.

At first light, Yusuf and Lina knelt beside the third step and ran their fingers along the joints of the wall. One block of coral stone, slightly paler than its neighbours, shifted under Yusuf's thumb with a gritty whisper. Together they eased it out, and behind it lay a small, dry hollow that no one in the family had known existed. Inside, wrapped carefully in a faded cotton cloth, was the pearl ledger, completely unharmed. Beneath it lay something neither of them had expected: a folded letter, its ink browned with age, addressed in a careful hand to "whoever finds this place after me." Lina let out a breath that was half laugh, half sob. "He wasn't losing it," she said. "He was saving it."

When they brought the ledger to breakfast, the room fell utterly silent, and then everyone began talking at once. Jiddo looked at the bundle in Yusuf's hands, and for a moment the fog in his eyes seemed to lift completely. "I heard the rain," he explained simply, "and I could not let the water take it a second time." Yusuf read the letter aloud: it had been written by Jiddo's own father, thanking his son for his courage during the flood and urging him to remember that a family's true wealth lies in honesty, not pearls. Uncle Faisal was quiet for a long while after that. Then he stood up, walked out to the courtyard, and apologised to Hamid with a sincerity that nobody in the family would ever forget.

On Thursday, the curator arrived and handled the ledger as though it were made of glass, promising that it would be displayed beside the letter and the story of its hiding place. Jiddo insisted that the secret niche should be preserved rather than sealed, and he asked Hamid, of all people, to build a small cedar door to cover it. The carpenter accepted the work with a smile that said more than any words could have. That evening, Yusuf sat on the third step as the call to Maghrib drifted across the rooftops of Al-Balad. He had always imagined that mysteries were solved by unmasking a villain, but this one had no villain at all, only a frightened boy from long ago and an old man who had never stopped protecting what he loved. Sometimes, Yusuf thought, the answer is hidden in plain sight, waiting for someone patient enough to listen.
