pages.text: In the oldest quarter of Jeddah, where coral-stone houses lean towards each other like elderly men sharing secrets, two rooftops face each other across a lane so narrow that a cat could leap from one to the other. Omar lived on the left side, and Rakan on the right, and for as long as either of them could remember, they had been inseparable. When they were eleven, bored during a long summer power cut, they had invented a code using nothing but two battered torches and a great deal of stubbornness. Long flashes, short flashes and carefully timed pauses could carry almost any message across the darkness. Their parents had assumed it was a phase that would fade, but five years later the lights still blinked between the two houses almost every night. By now the boys could hold entire conversations without saying a single word aloud.

Rakan lived with his grandfather, Jaddi Saleh, a quiet craftsman who repaired the carved wooden rawasheen that shaded the windows of the old houses. The workshop on the ground floor always smelled of sawdust and cardamom, and Omar had spent so many afternoons there that the old man treated him as a second grandson. 'A good lattice,' Jaddi Saleh liked to say, running his thumb along the delicate joints, 'holds together because every piece leans on another.' The boys would roll their eyes at this, having heard it a hundred times, but they never quite told him to stop. Each evening, after prayers and homework, they climbed to their rooftops and signalled the day's news: a teacher's terrible joke, a goal scored in the street, a plan for the weekend. It was, Omar would later realise, the steadiest thing in his life.

The trouble began in the autumn, when the regional robotics competition was announced. Omar and Rakan had been planning their entry for months, sketching designs on the backs of envelopes and arguing cheerfully over every gear and sensor. Then a group of older students from Omar's new school, who had won the competition twice before, invited him to join their team. Flattered and frankly dazzled, Omar accepted on the spot, and only afterwards did the weight of what he had done settle on his chest. Rather than face his friend, he sent a short message explaining that it was 'too good an opportunity to turn down'. The reply came within seconds and consisted of just two words: 'Go, then.' That night, for the first time in five years, the window across the lane stayed completely dark.

Weeks turned into months, and the silence hardened into something neither boy knew how to break. Omar shoved his torch into the back of a drawer, telling himself that he had outgrown childish games anyway. His new teammates were clever and confident, and the robot they built was undeniably impressive, yet working with them felt strangely hollow. Nobody laughed at his clumsy drawings or teased him when he got a calculation wrong; they simply corrected him and moved on. When they passed in the lane, Rakan would nod politely, which was somehow worse than if he had ignored Omar altogether. More than once, Omar found himself glancing at the dark window opposite before bed, half expecting a flicker that never came.

One sweltering night in early summer, a thick wall of dust rolled in from the desert, and shortly after midnight the electricity failed across the whole district. Unable to sleep in the airless heat, Omar climbed to the roof, hoping for even the faintest breeze. The city had vanished into a brownish haze, and the only light came from the occasional car crawling along a distant road. He was about to go back inside when something caught his eye: a weak, trembling glow in the window across the lane. Three short flashes, three long, three short, repeated over and over. Omar's breath caught in his throat, because he would have recognised that pattern anywhere.

He fumbled his way downstairs, tore open the drawer and dug out his old torch, praying the batteries had not died. When he flashed back the signal they had always used for 'I'm here', the reply came so fast that he almost dropped it. Slowly, letter by letter, he deciphered the message: 'JADDI FELL. CAN'T LIFT HIM. PHONE DEAD.' For a fraction of a second, an absurd thought crossed Omar's mind, that Rakan had not spoken to him in eight months. Then the thought evaporated, and he was hammering on his parents' door before he had even decided to move. 'Baba, wake up, it's Jaddi Saleh!' he shouted. His father, who had seen many emergencies in his years as a nurse, was pulling on his shoes before Omar had finished explaining.

They found the old man lying at the foot of the workshop stairs, conscious but grey with pain, while Rakan knelt beside him, gripping his hand. Omar's father examined him with calm, practised movements and announced that the hip was probably broken but that his breathing and pulse were steady. He called an ambulance on his own phone, then asked Omar to hold the torch steady so that he could see properly. In the circle of light, Rakan looked up, and for a long moment the two boys simply stared at each other. 'You answered,' Rakan whispered, as though he could hardly believe it. 'Of course I answered,' said Omar, and his voice cracked in a way he did not bother to hide.

The hospital corridor was cold and bright, and the boys sat side by side on hard plastic chairs while the doctors took Jaddi Saleh for an X-ray. For a while neither of them spoke, but eventually Rakan cleared his throat. 'I didn't really expect anyone to see,' he admitted. 'I just didn't know what else to do, so I kept flashing.' Omar stared at his hands and confessed that he had looked at Rakan's window almost every night since their quarrel. 'I was a coward,' he said quietly. 'I should have told you to your face, and I should never have abandoned our project in the first place.' Rakan gave a tired laugh and admitted that he had been checking Omar's window too, far too proud to be the one who blinked first.

By dawn, the doctors had confirmed a clean fracture that would heal well with surgery and patience. When the boys were finally allowed in, Jaddi Saleh was propped against his pillows, looking pale but distinctly pleased with himself. He studied the two of them standing together at the end of his bed and raised one bushy eyebrow. 'So,' he said, 'it took a broken old man to fix a broken friendship. I should have fallen down the stairs months ago.' The boys protested loudly, and he chuckled until the nurse warned him to rest. Before he closed his eyes, he murmured, 'Remember, a lattice holds because every piece leans on another,' and this time neither of them rolled their eyes.

A week later, with the electricity long restored and Jaddi Saleh recovering at home, Omar climbed to his rooftop just after the evening prayer. He had already told his teammates that he would help them prepare for the competition but would be entering next year with his original partner. Across the lane, a figure appeared, and a familiar light began to blink. Omar grinned as he decoded the message: 'NEW DESIGN. BETTER GEARS. YOUR DRAWINGS STILL TERRIBLE.' He flashed back a single word, the one they had always used to end their conversations, which meant something like 'always' in their private language. Then the two lights went on talking long into the night, steady and bright, two small stars hanging over the old city.

pages.text: Every morning in early spring, the clouds came down from the sky and walked through Grandfather Saleh's farm as though they owned it. Faisal had watched them all his life from the terraced slopes outside Abha, thick white fog drifting between the juniper trees, soaking his sleeves and beading on his eyelashes. Yet for all that moisture in the air, the ancient stone terraces below the house were cracking, and the coffee bushes his grandfather had tended for forty years were slowly losing their battle with the dry season. "The rain isn't what it used to be," Grandfather would say, running his weathered fingers over a brittle leaf. Faisal, sixteen and stubbornly practical, had never been one to accept a problem simply because it was old. Standing in the fog one morning, feeling it cling to his skin, a question struck him with almost physical force: what if the water they needed wasn't falling from the sky at all, but floating right in front of them?

That evening, Faisal buried himself in research papers until well past midnight. He discovered that in the coastal deserts of Chile and Morocco, villages had been harvesting fog for years using vast vertical nets made of fine plastic mesh. As fog passes through the mesh, tiny droplets collide with the fibres, merge together, and eventually grow heavy enough to trickle down into gutters below. Some installations were reportedly collecting hundreds of litres a day, enough to sustain entire communities. "It's almost too simple," he muttered, scribbling calculations in the margin of his notebook. His older sister Noura, who was studying statistics at university and rarely missed an opportunity to tease him, peered over his shoulder. "Simple ideas are usually the ones that either change everything or fail spectacularly," she said, "so you had better collect proper data if you want anyone to take you seriously."

When Faisal presented his proposal for the regional science fair, the reaction from his classmates was, to put it mildly, lukewarm. Turki, who had won the previous year with an elaborate solar-powered irrigation system, leaned back in his chair with an unmistakable smirk. "You're going to catch clouds with a fishing net?" he asked, and half the room burst out laughing. Faisal felt his cheeks burn, but before he could respond, their teacher, Ustadh Hamad, raised a hand for silence. "Every serious scientific idea sounds ridiculous to someone at first," he said calmly, "so the question isn't whether it sounds strange, but whether the evidence supports it." He agreed to supervise the project on one condition: Faisal had to design a rigorous experiment, with measurements taken every single day for six weeks.

Grandfather Saleh listened to the plan in thoughtful silence, sipping his cardamom-scented coffee, and Faisal braced himself for polite scepticism. Instead, the old man set down his cup and smiled in a way Faisal had not seen for months. "When I was a boy," he said, "my own grandfather used to leave flat stones beneath certain trees, and in the morning they would be wet even when no rain had fallen. We thought it was a blessing from Allah, and perhaps it was, but perhaps He also gave us minds to understand how it worked." Together they spent the following weekend building three collectors from wooden posts, sheets of double-layered mesh, and sections of plastic guttering salvaged from an old storeroom. They positioned them along the ridge where the fog was thickest, each one angled to face the prevailing wind. By sunset, Faisal's hands were blistered and his back ached, but he could hardly wait for morning.

The first dawn was a revelation. Faisal ran up the slope in the half-light, his breath forming small clouds of its own, and found clear water dripping steadily from the gutters into the containers below. He measured the contents with trembling hands: just under four litres from the first collector, a little over three from the second, and almost five from the third. It was hardly enough to revive a whole farm, yet it was undeniably real, water drawn from what had seemed like empty air. Noura, who had insisted on joining him, recorded every figure alongside the temperature, humidity, and wind speed. "Don't get carried away," she warned, though she was grinning too. "One good morning is an anecdote, not a result."

The second week brought a setback that nearly ended everything. A violent storm swept in from the west one night, and by morning two of the three collectors lay flattened in the mud, their mesh torn to shreds and their posts snapped like matchsticks. Faisal stood among the wreckage, utterly deflated, unable to speak for several minutes. "Perhaps Turki was right," he finally admitted, kicking at a broken gutter. "Perhaps this was a fantasy all along." Grandfather Saleh placed a heavy hand on his shoulder and said nothing for a while, gazing out at the valley. "These terraces were built stone by stone by men who watched floods wash away their work a hundred times," he said at last. "They did not give up, so neither will you."

Rather than simply rebuilding, Faisal decided to treat the disaster as data. He analysed the damage and realised that the rigid frames had acted like sails, catching the full force of the gusts until something had to give. Working late into the evenings, he redesigned the collectors with flexible joints and tension cables anchored deep into the rocky soil, allowing the structures to bend without breaking. He also experimented with a tighter mesh weave after reading that smaller gaps could capture finer droplets, a modification that turned out to be crucial. Ustadh Hamad visited the farm to inspect the new design and nodded approvingly. "Failure is simply information you haven't learned to use yet," he remarked. When the next storm arrived ten days later, all three collectors swayed and creaked, but every one of them was still standing at dawn.

By the end of the six weeks, the notebook was crammed with figures, and Noura spent an entire weekend transforming them into graphs. The results exceeded even Faisal's most optimistic predictions: the redesigned collectors averaged nearly eleven litres each per foggy morning, more than double the yield of the original models. Noura also uncovered a striking pattern, showing that the highest yields occurred when the wind blew steadily from the southwest at moderate speeds. "You see?" she said, tapping the screen. "This isn't luck, it's a predictable relationship, which means you could position future collectors far more efficiently." Faisal stared at the neat lines climbing across the chart and felt something shift inside him. For the first time, he truly understood that science was not about being right at the start, but about being honest enough to keep testing until the truth revealed itself.

At the regional science fair, Faisal's stand was modest compared with the gleaming robots and elaborate screens around it: just a scaled-down collector, a misting machine borrowed from a garden centre, and Noura's carefully printed graphs. Yet as the morning progressed, a crowd gradually gathered, and the judges lingered far longer than he had dared to hope. One of them, an environmental engineer from a university in Jeddah, questioned him relentlessly about mesh density, maintenance costs, and how the system might be scaled across the mountainous south. Faisal answered every question, admitting openly where his knowledge ran out. When the results were announced that afternoon, his project was awarded first prize, and the engineer invited him to visit her research laboratory during the summer holidays. Turki was among the first to approach him afterwards, and to Faisal's surprise, he extended his hand. "I owe you an apology," he said sheepishly, "and honestly, I'd love to know whether my solar pumps could move your water uphill."

Months later, on a cool morning when the fog lay thick across the valley, Faisal and his grandfather walked together along the terraces. Water from a row of twelve collectors now flowed through a network of pipes into a small stone reservoir, and from there to the roots of the coffee bushes, which had begun to put out glossy new leaves. Turki's solar pump hummed quietly beside the tank, the two rivals having become, somewhat unexpectedly, firm friends and collaborators. Grandfather Saleh stopped beside a bush heavy with young green berries and cradled one gently in his palm. "My grandfather's wet stones were the beginning of an answer," he said softly, "and you have finished the sentence he started." Faisal looked up at the clouds drifting through the junipers, no longer seeing them as something that merely passed by. They were, he realised, a gift that had been waiting patiently all along for someone curious enough to catch it.

pages.text: Faisal had spent most of his sixteen years believing that the Empty Quarter was simply a blank space on the map, a place people mentioned only to illustrate the idea of nothingness. So when his uncle Majid, a geologist at the university in Riyadh, invited him on a research trip to the Wabar craters, he accepted mainly because it would make an impressive story at school. What he hadn't bargained for was his grandfather insisting on coming along. "I crossed those sands before your uncle was born," the old man announced at dinner, in a tone that made it clear the matter was closed. Faisal exchanged a doubtful glance with his uncle, but neither of them dared to argue. Grandfather's eyesight was no longer what it had been, yet his stubbornness, it seemed, had only grown sharper with age.

They set off before dawn, the four-wheel drive loaded with water, fuel and enough scientific equipment to fill a small laboratory. Faisal sat in the back with a satellite navigation device on his knees, tracking their progress with the quiet satisfaction of someone who trusts technology completely. Every so often, Grandfather would lean towards the window and murmur something about the shape of a dune or the direction its ridges were facing. "The wind writes on the sand every night," he said, "and anyone who can read it will never be lost." Faisal smiled politely, though privately he considered such advice charmingly outdated. After all, why would anyone need to read the wind when a satellite could tell you your position to within three metres? He would later look back on that thought with considerable embarrassment.

By early afternoon, they had reached the craters, a series of shallow hollows half-swallowed by the restless sand. Scattered across the ground were glossy black fragments that glittered in the harsh light like broken pieces of night. "Impact glass," Uncle Majid explained, crouching to pick one up. "When the meteorite struck, the heat was so intense that it melted the sand instantly." Grandfather nodded slowly and told them that, according to the old stories, a proud city had once stood here before fire fell from the sky. Faisal pointed out that scientists had dated the impact to only a few centuries ago, and that no city had ever been found. "Perhaps," Grandfather replied with a faint smile, "but a story doesn't have to be true about the past to be true about people."

It was Grandfather who noticed the change first, long before any of the instruments did. The air had grown unnaturally still, and on the southern horizon a dull brown haze was creeping upwards like smoke from a distant fire. "We need to secure everything now, not in ten minutes," he said, and for once nobody questioned him. They had barely managed to pack the equipment and shelter inside the vehicle when the storm hit with a roar that drowned out all conversation. Sand hammered against the windows so fiercely that Faisal half expected the glass to crack. For hours they sat in the stifling darkness, sipping water sparingly and listening to the desert rage around them. Somewhere in the middle of the night, exhausted by fear as much as by heat, Faisal finally drifted into an uneasy sleep.

When dawn came, the silence was almost more unsettling than the storm had been. Forcing open the door, they discovered that sand had piled up against one side of the vehicle, burying the wheels almost to the axles. Worse still, the satellite phone, which had been strapped to the roof rack, had vanished entirely, and the navigation device refused to switch on. "The battery must have overheated," Uncle Majid muttered, shaking it as though that might somehow bring it back to life. While digging out the rear wheel, he stepped awkwardly into a hollow and twisted his ankle so badly that he could barely put any weight on it. Faisal felt his stomach tighten as the reality of their situation sank in. They were in the middle of the largest sand desert on earth, with no map, no signal and only one driver who could still use both feet.

"You'll have to drive," Uncle Majid said quietly, handing Faisal the keys. Faisal had practised in the desert near their farm, but never in terrain like this, and he was painfully aware that a single mistake could leave them stranded for good. It took the three of them over two hours to free the vehicle, with Uncle Majid hopping between the wheels to lay down the metal boards and Grandfather directing the work as calmly as if he were organising a family picnic. When at last the engine growled and the tyres gripped the sand, Faisal let out a breath he hadn't realised he'd been holding. "Good," said Grandfather, settling into the front passenger seat. "Now, if you're willing to listen to an old man's outdated advice, I'll take you home." Faisal had the grace to blush, and he didn't argue.

Grandfather couldn't see the dunes clearly, so he asked Faisal to describe them in detail: which side was steep, which side was gentle, how the ripples curved across the surface. From these descriptions he pieced together the direction of the prevailing wind and, from that, the route they needed to follow. "Keep the long slopes on your right," he instructed, "and never try to climb a slip face, however tempting the shortcut looks." Twice Faisal was convinced they were heading the wrong way, and twice he bit his tongue and trusted the old man's judgement. Gradually, he began to notice patterns he had been blind to only a day earlier, as if someone had quietly translated the landscape into a language he could understand. By late afternoon, he was reading the sand almost before Grandfather asked him to.

Just as the sun was beginning to sink, a deep, low hum rose from somewhere ahead of them, so powerful that Faisal felt it vibrating through the steering wheel. He slammed on the brakes, convinced that something had gone terribly wrong with the engine. Grandfather, however, laughed out loud for the first time since the storm. "That's the singing dune," he said, his voice thick with emotion. "I heard it when I was younger than you, travelling with my father's caravan, and I never thought I'd hear it again." Uncle Majid explained that when sand of exactly the right size slides down a dune, the grains vibrate together and produce a sound like a distant engine or a deep musical note. To Faisal, though, the scientific explanation did nothing to diminish the wonder of it. More importantly, Grandfather now knew precisely where they were: the old caravan track lay less than a night's drive to the north.

Driving through the desert at night was a risk, but with their water supply running dangerously low, waiting until morning was hardly an option. Grandfather told Faisal to look for al-Jadi, the star that never moves, which travellers have used to find the north for thousands of years. Faisal found it with surprising ease, a steady point of light hanging above the darkness like a promise. Mile after mile, he kept it framed in the top corner of the windscreen, adjusting his course whenever the dunes forced him to swerve. Uncle Majid dozed fitfully in the back, his ankle propped up on a bag, while Grandfather recited verses of poetry under his breath to keep Faisal awake. Never in his life had Faisal concentrated so hard, nor felt so strangely calm.

Not long before dawn, a flicker of orange appeared on the horizon, and Faisal's heart leapt into his throat. As they drew closer, it turned out to be a campfire belonging to a family of camel herders who had pitched their tent beside the track. Without asking a single question, the herders welcomed them in, poured them bitter cardamom coffee and pressed handfuls of dates into their hands. One of the young men had a working phone, and within minutes Uncle Majid was reassuring his anxious wife that they were safe. The eldest herder listened to the story of the storm and then turned to Faisal with an approving nod. "You drove by the stars," he said. "Your grandfather has taught you well." Faisal glanced at Grandfather, who was pretending, quite unsuccessfully, not to look proud.

Back in Riyadh a week later, Faisal stood in front of his class to present his project on the Wabar craters. He described the meteorite, the impact glass and the physics of the singing dune, but he also told them about reading the wind and steering by al-Jadi. "I used to think that science and tradition were rivals," he concluded, "but out there I learnt that they're really two ways of paying attention to the same world." That evening, Grandfather called him into the majlis and placed a small piece of black glass in his palm. "I picked this up at the craters," he said, "so that you would never forget the night you learnt to see." Faisal turned it over in the lamplight, watching it gleam like a fragment of the desert sky. He knew, with absolute certainty, that he never would.

grammar.ar: نستخدم تراكيب التنازل للاعتراف بنقطة الطرف الآخر قبل الرد عليها، مما يجعل حجتنا أكثر إقناعاً واحتراماً. تأتي Granted و Admittedly في بداية الجملة يليها فاصلة، ثم نستخدم however أو yet أو but لتقديم الرد. أما While فتربط جملتين في جملة واحدة: While + الجزء المُعترف به، ثم الرأي المعاكس. تجنّب استخدام although و but معاً في الجملة نفسها كما يحدث أحياناً بتأثير العربية (رغم... لكن).
examples: Granted, phones can be misused; however, they also give instant access to information.
While I take your point about concentration, I'd argue that phones can be stored during tests.
Admittedly, some students lack self-control, yet that's an argument for better guidance, not a ban.

words.ex: The underlying assumption is that all online interaction is shallow.
Saying that all teenagers are addicted to their phones is a sweeping generalisation.
We must distinguish between correlation and causation when interpreting these statistics.
You can disagree strongly without being confrontational.
The issue is far more nuanced than the headline suggests.

words.w: to take something at face value
words.ar: يأخذ الأمر على ظاهره دون تمحيص
words.ex: We shouldn't take claims from viral posts at face value.

dialogue.t: It's obvious, really. Social media makes teenagers less social. They'd rather text than talk.
That's an interesting view, but that presupposes that texting isn't a genuine form of social interaction.
Well, it isn't the same as meeting face to face, is it?
Perhaps not, but isn't it rather the case that many teenagers use social media to arrange the very meetings you're describing?
Maybe, but I've read that teenagers today spend less time with friends than previous generations did.
I'm not entirely convinced that social media is the cause, though. Couldn't it be heavier homework loads or fewer public spaces?
Hmm, I suppose there could be other factors.
Exactly. And what evidence is there to suggest that it's the platforms themselves, rather than how they're used, that's the problem?

grammar.title: Negative Questions and Softeners for Polite Challenges
grammar.ar: عند الاعتراض على رأي ما بأدب، نستخدم الأسئلة المنفية مثل Isn't it rather the case that...? فهي تقترح فكرة بديلة دون أن تفرضها. كما نستخدم كلمات مُلطِّفة مثل entirely و rather و perhaps لتخفيف حدة الاعتراض. فعبارة I'm not entirely convinced أكثر لباقة بكثير من I don't agree. في الإنجليزية الأكاديمية يُعدّ الاعتراض المباشر جداً فظّاً، حتى لو كان مقبولاً في سياقات أخرى.
examples: Isn't it rather the case that loneliness existed long before social media?
I'm not entirely convinced that screen time alone explains the decline.
Wouldn't it be fairer to say that the effects vary from person to person?

words.ex: Some fear that traditional textbooks will soon become obsolete.
AI can already automate tasks like marking multiple-choice tests.

words.ar: لا يمكن الاستغناء عنه / لا بديل له
words.ex: A teacher's ability to inspire students is arguably irreplaceable.
It's difficult to speculate about how classrooms will look in thirty years.
I can't see robots running schools in the foreseeable future.
AI is more likely to augment teachers' work than to replace it.

dialogue.t: Do you think AI will eventually replace teachers?
Completely? It's highly unlikely that machines will take over every aspect of teaching, at least in the foreseeable future.
But AI tutors are improving incredibly quickly.
True, and there's every chance that they'll handle routine tasks like marking and grammar practice.
So teachers' roles are going to change?
Absolutely. The role is bound to evolve. I'd be inclined to think teachers will become more like mentors and coaches.
Could some schools try to operate with hardly any human staff?
It's conceivable that a few might experiment with it, but I doubt parents would accept that for long.

grammar.title: Expressing Degrees of Certainty
grammar.ar: تستخدم الإنجليزية عبارات مختلفة للتعبير عن درجة اليقين بشأن المستقبل. فعبارة is bound to تعني أن الأمر شبه مؤكد، وThere's every chance that تعني احتمالاً كبيراً جداً، بينما It's conceivable that تعني أنه ممكن لكنه غير مرجّح، وIt's highly unlikely that تعني احتمالاً ضعيفاً جداً. أما I'd be inclined to think فتعبّر عن رأي شخصي بحذر. لاحظ أن bound يتبعها to + المصدر، بينما تتبع العبارات الأخرى that + جملة كاملة.
examples: AI is bound to play a bigger role in education over the next decade.
There's every chance that personalised learning apps will become standard in schools.
It's conceivable that some subjects could be taught entirely online, but it's highly unlikely to happen everywhere.

words.ex: Her speech really resonated with the younger members of the audience.
He opened with a rhetorical question to grab the judges' attention.
These figures underscore the urgency of the problem.

words.ar: التراخي / الرضا المفرط عن الوضع الراهن
words.ex: Complacency is the biggest threat to progress in any society.
We are living through a pivotal moment in our nation's history.
She repeated the key statistic at the end to drive her point home.

dialogue.t: I'm giving a speech at debate club tomorrow about reading for pleasure, but my draft sounds a bit flat. Can I try my opening on you?
Of course. Go ahead.
Never before has our generation had so much information at our fingertips, yet so little patience to read a single book.
That's a powerful start. The inversion really grabs attention. What comes next?
What really matters is not how much we scroll, but how deeply we think. And it is books that train us to think deeply.
Excellent. You might also challenge the idea that reading is old-fashioned.
Good idea. How about this: Far from being outdated, reading actually gives us an edge in a world full of distractions.
Perfect. Then finish strongly with something like: The last thing we need is a generation that has forgotten how to focus.

grammar.title: Cleft Sentences and Negative Inversion
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجمل المشطورة (Cleft sentences) لتسليط الضوء على معلومة معينة: It is + العنصر المؤكَّد + that...، أو What + جملة + is/was.... أما القلب بعد الظروف السلبية مثل Never before و Rarely و Seldom فيُضفي طابعاً رسمياً ودرامياً على الخطاب، ويتطلب وضع الفعل المساعد قبل الفاعل. هذه الأساليب شائعة في الخطب والمناظرات لأنها تجعل الأفكار الرئيسية بارزة ومؤثرة.
examples: It is young people who will shape the future of our country, not the machines we build.
What really matters is how we act, not what we promise.
Never before has it been so important to think critically about what we read online.

words.ex: Traffic congestion in major cities costs the economy billions every year.
Investing in public transport infrastructure creates long-term value.
A sustainable city reduces its reliance on private cars.
Building more highways often encourages urban sprawl.

words.ar: الطلب المُحفَّز (زيادة الطلب نتيجة زيادة العرض)
words.ex: Because of induced demand, new roads often fill up with traffic within a few years.
Her rebuttal exposed the weaknesses in her opponent's figures.

dialogue.t: To open, I'd like to put forward the case that Saudi cities should prioritise public transport over new roads. The Riyadh Metro shows what is possible when we invest in sustainable infrastructure.
Thank you. I'd argue the opposite. Our cities are spread out, summers are extremely hot, and most families depend on cars. New roads meet people's real needs.
My opponent claims that families depend on cars, but that dependence exists precisely because alternatives have been limited until now.
That may be so, but people won't walk to a metro station in forty-five-degree heat.
Which is exactly why modern systems include air-conditioned stations, feeder buses and park-and-ride facilities. Besides, induced demand means new roads simply fill up again.
Weighing everything up, I still believe a balanced approach is needed. We can't abandon road development entirely.
Nobody is suggesting abandoning roads. But on balance, the evidence clearly points to public transport as the more sustainable solution for growing cities.
A fair summary, though I'd say the debate is far from settled.

grammar.title: Discourse Markers for Structuring a Debate
grammar.ar: تساعد أدوات الربط في تنظيم المناظرة إلى مراحل واضحة: الافتتاح، والرد، والخاتمة. نستخدم في الافتتاح عبارات مثل To open, I'd like to put forward، وفي الرد My opponent claims..., but، وفي الخاتمة Weighing everything up أو On balance. تُعطي هذه العبارات المستمعين إشارات واضحة عن الانتقال من مرحلة إلى أخرى، مما يجعل الحجة أسهل في المتابعة وأكثر إقناعاً.
examples: To open, I'd like to put forward three reasons why public transport deserves priority.
My opponent claims that roads reduce travel time, but studies show the effect is only temporary.
On balance, the evidence clearly points to investment in metro and bus networks.

words.ex: A good opening should captivate your audience within the first thirty seconds.
Before going into detail, I'll briefly outline the three main stages of the project.
Clear signposting helps listeners follow the structure of a long presentation.
NEOM is one of the most ambitious urban projects ever attempted.
The Red Sea Project aims to be a model of sustainable tourism.
She opened her talk with a striking statistic about renewable energy.

dialogue.t: Right, you've got two minutes for your introduction. Whenever you're ready.
Thank you. Let me start with a striking fact: the Red Sea Project covers an area larger than some entire countries.
I'd like to begin by explaining why this project matters for Saudi Arabia's future beyond oil.
Over the next few minutes, I'll take you through its goals, its environmental commitments and its challenges.
Firstly, I'll outline the vision behind the project, then move on to how it protects coral reefs and marine life.
That was very clear. Your opening fact really grabbed my attention.
Thanks! Do you think my signposting was too obvious, though?
Not at all. In a formal presentation, the audience appreciates knowing exactly where you're heading.

grammar.title: Prepositions followed by -ing forms
grammar.ar: عندما يأتي فعل بعد حرف جر مثل by أو with أو after أو before فإنه يأخذ صيغة ‎-ing‎ وليس المصدر. هذا شائع جدًا في عبارات تنظيم العرض مثل I'd like to begin by explaining. انتبه: كثير من المتعلمين العرب يقولون begin by explain، والصحيح begin by explaining.
examples: I'd like to begin by giving you some background on NEOM.
After describing the project's goals, I'll move on to its challenges.
I'll finish by summarising the key points.

words.ex: Saudi Arabia is one of the world's largest producers of water through desalination.
Reverse osmosis forces seawater through a membrane to remove the salt.
The membrane allows water molecules to pass but blocks salt particles.
Before treatment, the seawater contains sand, algae and other impurities.
Disposing of brine safely is one of the main environmental challenges.
Seawater is pumped from the coast into large intake tanks.

dialogue.t: Imagine I know nothing about science. How does a desalination plant actually work?
The process essentially involves removing salt and impurities from seawater so that it's safe to drink.
First, seawater is pumped into the plant and filtered to remove sand and larger particles.
Once the water has been filtered, it is then pushed at high pressure through special membranes.
And what do those membranes do exactly?
To put it simply, they act like an extremely fine sieve. In other words, water gets through, but salt doesn't.
This is followed by adding minerals back into the water, and finally it's sent to homes through pipelines.
Excellent. The sieve comparison made it much easier to understand.

grammar.title: The passive voice for describing processes
grammar.ar: نستخدم المبني للمجهول عند وصف العمليات لأن التركيز يكون على ما يحدث وليس على من يقوم به. يتكوّن من فعل be بالزمن المناسب مع التصريف الثالث للفعل. ويمكن استخدام المضارع التام المبني للمجهول (has been + التصريف الثالث) لإظهار أن خطوة اكتملت قبل الخطوة التالية.
examples: The seawater is filtered to remove sand and algae.
Once the salt has been removed, minerals are added to the water.
The brine is then returned to the sea through long pipes.

words.ex: Food waste is a pressing issue in many Gulf countries.
The surplus food from the wedding was donated to a local charity.
Composting leftovers at school is a viable and low-cost solution.
Food banks redistribute unused meals to families in need.
We launched a campaign to raise awareness about portion sizes during Eid.
The school plans to implement the new recycling scheme next term.

dialogue.t: So, what problem have you chosen to focus on?
One of the most pressing issues in our community is food waste during celebrations like weddings and Ramadan gatherings.
If left unaddressed, it will keep costing families money and putting extra pressure on landfill sites.
That's a big cultural issue, though. Generosity is important to people. How would you tackle it?
A viable solution would be to partner with food banks that collect surplus food straight after events.
This would not only reduce waste but also help families who struggle to afford proper meals.
It's essential that the food be collected quickly and stored safely, so hygiene rules must be clear.
That's well justified. You respect the tradition of generosity while making it more responsible.

grammar.title: The subjunctive after essential, vital and recommend
grammar.ar: بعد عبارات مثل It's essential that و It's vital that وأفعال مثل recommend و suggest نستخدم المصدر المجرد للفعل دون to ودون إضافة s، حتى مع he وshe وit. وفي المبني للمجهول نستخدم be بدلًا من is أو are. هذا الأسلوب رسمي ويضفي قوة على اقتراحاتك في العروض.
examples: It's essential that leftover food be stored at the correct temperature.
I recommend that the school introduce a no-waste policy at events.
It's vital that every student understand the impact of food waste.

words.ex: Failing my first driving test was a frustrating setback.
Even when the training got harder, she decided to persevere.
Joining the debate club was a real turning point in my life.
Speaking in front of the whole school felt incredibly daunting.
The experience taught me resilience and patience.
I felt completely overwhelmed by the amount of work.

dialogue.t: Tell me about a challenge that really changed you.
Two years ago, I broke my leg just before the national swimming trials. Little did I know that it would change my whole outlook.
At first, I felt overwhelmed and honestly quite angry. It was only when I started helping coach younger swimmers that I realised how much I loved teaching.
That's quite a turning point. What was the hardest part?
Watching my teammates compete without me. But what struck me most was how much they still valued my advice.
Looking back, the injury taught me that resilience isn't just about winning races.
Had I not been injured, I would never have discovered my passion for coaching.
What a powerful ending. Your audience would definitely remember that.

grammar.title: Inversion for dramatic effect
grammar.ar: في القلب (Inversion) نضع الفعل المساعد قبل الفاعل لإضفاء أثر درامي ورسمي على السرد. يحدث ذلك بعد عبارات نفي أو تقييد مثل Little أو Never أو Only when. كما يمكن حذف if في الشرط الثالث وقلب الجملة: Had I not بدلًا من If I hadn't.
examples: Little did I know that this small decision would change everything.
Had I given up, I would never have reached the final.
Only when I failed did I understand the value of preparation.

words.ex: Could you clarify what you meant by long-term impact?
The examiner asked me to elaborate on my second point.
If a question is confusing, it's fine to rephrase it before answering.
That's a valid point, and I hadn't considered it before.

words.w: off the top of my head
words.ex: Off the top of my head, I'd say around forty percent.
A confident speaker acknowledges the limits of their knowledge.

dialogue.t: Thanks for the presentation. Isn't desalination too expensive and harmful to justify on such a large scale?
That's a really interesting question; let me think about it for a moment.
If I understand you correctly, you're asking whether the benefits outweigh the financial and environmental costs.
Exactly. Especially the impact on marine life.
You've raised a valid point. I'd need to look into that further, but I know newer plants use solar energy to cut costs.
But earlier you said the brine was harmless. Isn't that contradictory?
To clarify what I meant, the brine is harmless only when it's diluted properly before being returned to the sea.
Good recovery. You stayed calm and handled the follow-up question well.

grammar.title: Indirect questions
grammar.ar: عند إعادة صياغة سؤال أحدهم أو طرح سؤال بلطف نستخدم السؤال غير المباشر، وفيه يأتي الفاعل قبل الفعل كما في الجملة الخبرية، ولا نستخدم do أو does أو did. ونستخدم whether أو if عندما يكون السؤال الأصلي بنعم أو لا. مثال: you're asking whether it is وليس you're asking is it.
examples: If I understand you correctly, you're asking whether the project is affordable.
Could you tell me what you mean by sustainable?
You're wondering how the plant deals with the brine.

words.ex: I'm thinking of choosing computer engineering as my major.
The job prospects for data scientists are excellent.
Renewable energy engineers are increasingly in demand in the region.
She hopes to pursue a career in medicine.
The university has cutting-edge laboratories for AI research.
Teaching can be a demanding but highly rewarding career.

dialogue.t: Today I'll be talking about why I want to pursue a degree in artificial intelligence.
What drew me to AI is its potential to solve real problems, from diagnosing diseases to managing traffic in cities like Riyadh.
This field is becoming increasingly important, and specialists are in demand both locally and globally.
Ultimately, I want a career that is both cutting-edge and genuinely rewarding.
To conclude, I'd like to leave you with this thought: technology is only as good as the people who design it. Are there any questions?
Yes. What would you do if AI started replacing jobs in your own field?
That's a really interesting question. I'd say the key is to keep learning, because what AI can't replace is human judgement and creativity.
A thoughtful answer and a very well-structured presentation overall. Well done.

grammar.title: Cleft sentences with What
grammar.ar: الجملة المشقوقة (Cleft sentence) التي تبدأ بـ What تُستخدم لتسليط الضوء على معلومة مهمة وجذب انتباه الجمهور إليها. تتكوّن من What + جملة + is/was + المعلومة المراد التركيز عليها. هذا الأسلوب مفيد جدًا في العروض لإبراز الأفكار الرئيسية بدلًا من الجمل العادية.
examples: What drew me to medicine is the chance to make a real difference.
What surprised me most was how many careers involve data analysis.
What I'd like to emphasise is the importance of practical experience.

words.ex: The credibility of the article was undermined when readers discovered the author had no medical training.
Before you share a health tip, check whether it's backed by peer-reviewed research.

words.ar: أدلة قائمة على تجارب شخصية (غير علمية)
words.ex: Her claim that the diet cured her headaches is purely anecdotal evidence, not proof.
Several scientists have debunked the myth that eating late at night automatically makes you gain weight.
The headline was misleading because the study had only been carried out on mice.
There's a clear conflict of interest when a company funds research into its own product.

dialogue.t: Have you seen that viral post claiming that drinking lemon water first thing in the morning burns belly fat?
Yes, my aunt shared it in the family group. But the credibility of a claim like that hinges on where it comes from, and the post doesn't cite a single study.
True. And it's worth bearing in mind that the account that posted it is also selling a so-called detox lemon kit.
Exactly, that's a blatant conflict of interest. Honestly, this claim doesn't stand up to scrutiny because no food can target fat in one specific part of the body.
I suppose it might encourage people to drink more water, though, which can't be a bad thing.
Fair point. But if we wanted to be certain, we'd need to cross-check the claim against peer-reviewed research or official guidance from the Ministry of Health.
Agreed. Let's look it up on a reputable medical website before anyone else forwards it.

grammar.title: Hedging: expressing caution and tentativeness
grammar.ar: في النقاش الأكاديمي نتجنب الأحكام المطلقة ونستخدم لغة التحفّظ لإظهار الدقة والموضوعية. نستخدم أفعالًا مساعدة مثل may وmight وcould، وأفعالًا مثل appear وseem وsuggest وtend to، وظروفًا مثل arguably وpossibly. هذا يجعل رأيك أكثر إقناعًا لأنه يعترف بحدود الأدلة المتاحة.
examples: The study appears to suggest a link between sugar and poor sleep, but the sample was very small.
This supplement may help some people, although the evidence is far from conclusive.
It could be argued that influencers tend to exaggerate the benefits of the products they promote.

words.ex: There has been a marked increase in the number of international visitors to AlUla.
The chart shows a surge in hotel bookings during Riyadh Season.
Visitor numbers fluctuated throughout the year, peaking in the winter months.
Leisure tourism now accounts for a much larger share of total visits than it did a decade ago.
A growing proportion of entertainment spending comes from young Saudis.
The most plausible explanation for the dip in 2020 is the global pandemic.

dialogue.t: Looking at this chart, there has been a marked rise in tourist arrivals since 2019. The line is almost flat before that.
That can largely be attributed to the introduction of tourist e-visas in 2019. Before then, it was quite difficult to visit the Kingdom purely for leisure.
Right. And there's that sharp drop in 2020, which obviously reflects the pandemic, followed by a steady rise from 2021 onwards.
What strikes me is the entertainment bar. According to the chart, domestic visitors account for roughly two-thirds of attendance at major events.
Interesting. One plausible explanation is that young Saudis who used to travel abroad for concerts and theme parks can now enjoy them at home.
That makes sense. The creation of the General Entertainment Authority in 2016 probably laid the foundations for all of this.
Although we should be careful. The chart shows correlation, but it doesn't prove exactly which factor mattered most.

grammar.title: Describing trends: adjective + noun vs verb + adverb
grammar.ar: عند وصف البيانات يمكننا التعبير عن الاتجاه بطريقتين: اسم مع صفة (there was a sharp rise in …) أو فعل مع ظرف (… rose sharply). التنويع بين الطريقتين يجعل وصفك أكثر احترافية. كما نستخدم حروف الجر بدقة: rise by (مقدار التغيّر) وrise to (القيمة النهائية) وa rise of (حجم الزيادة).
examples: There was a steady increase in visitor numbers between 2021 and 2023.
Visitor numbers increased steadily between 2021 and 2023.
Spending on entertainment rose by 40% to reach its highest level in 2023.

words.ex: Rising rents have had a knock-on effect on where young families choose to live.
Urban sprawl means many residents now spend over an hour commuting each day.
The rapid growth in population has put a strain on water and electricity supplies.
Replacing green spaces with concrete exacerbates the urban heat island effect.
Investment in public transport infrastructure, such as the Riyadh Metro, is meant to ease congestion.
Car-dependent cities tend to encourage a more sedentary lifestyle.

dialogue.t: Riyadh has changed so much in the last ten years. The rapid growth has given rise to some serious challenges, hasn't it?
Definitely. As a direct consequence of so many people moving to the city, demand for housing has soared and rents have gone through the roof.
And a lot of the traffic problem stems from urban sprawl. New neighbourhoods are built further and further out.
Exactly. People end up driving everywhere. This, in turn, leads to more pollution and a more sedentary lifestyle.
I'd add the heat as well. More concrete and fewer trees exacerbate the urban heat island effect.
That's partly why projects like Green Riyadh are so important. Had the city invested in public transport earlier, congestion would probably be far less severe today.
True, but now that the Metro is running, it'll be interesting to see whether people actually change their habits.

grammar.title: Inverted and mixed conditionals
grammar.ar: في الأسلوب الرسمي يمكن حذف if في الجملة الشرطية الثالثة وتقديم had على الفاعل: Had the city planned… بدلًا من If the city had planned…. أما الشرط المختلط فيربط حدثًا في الماضي بنتيجة في الحاضر: had + التصريف الثالث في جملة الشرط، وwould + المصدر في جملة الجواب. نستخدم هذه التراكيب لتحليل الأسباب والنتائج بطريقة أكاديمية.
examples: Had the government not invested in the Metro, traffic would be even worse today.
Had planners protected more green spaces, the city would have stayed cooler last summer.
If Riyadh hadn't expanded so quickly, housing would be more affordable now.

words.ex: From my grandfather's standpoint, a government job was the ultimate sign of success.
Older generations often valued job security over personal fulfilment.

words.ar: ريادي / ذو روح المبادرة في الأعمال
words.ex: Many young Saudis are increasingly entrepreneurial and dream of launching their own start-ups.
Medicine and engineering have traditionally carried a great deal of prestige in our society.
There used to be a stigma attached to working in certain jobs, but attitudes are changing.
My sister chose graphic design because she wanted a career that would give her a sense of fulfilment.

dialogue.t: I asked my grandfather what success meant to him, and he said it was having a stable government job and supporting the whole family.
That's typical. Whereas older generations tend to prioritise job security, younger people are often more interested in passion and flexibility.
But I can understand his view. From his standpoint, he grew up when opportunities were limited, so stability really mattered.
Absolutely. I think there's a fundamental difference in how each generation sees risk. My cousin quit a secure job to start a coffee business, and my uncle was horrified.
Still, if you think about it, both views share the assumption that education opens doors. They just disagree about which doors are worth opening.
That's a fair way to put it. And to be honest, neither side is entirely right. Passion without a plan can be just as risky as security without satisfaction.
Agreed. Maybe the ideal is combining my grandfather's sense of responsibility with our generation's ambition.

grammar.title: Linkers of contrast: whereas, while, by contrast, on the other hand
grammar.ar: نستخدم whereas وwhile لربط فكرتين متقابلتين داخل جملة واحدة، ويمكن أن يأتيا في بداية الجملة أو وسطها. أما by contrast وon the other hand فيأتيان عادة في بداية جملة جديدة يليهما فاصلة. لاحظ أن whereas أكثر رسمية من while، وتستخدم للمقارنة الواضحة بين طرفين.
examples: Whereas my parents studied what their families expected, I chose my own major.
My father values a fixed salary, while my brother prefers freelance work.
Older generations saw success as financial stability. By contrast, many teenagers today link it to personal happiness.

words.ex: Doctors face a real dilemma when a treatment could save a life but carries serious risks.
Apps should never collect personal data without the user's informed consent.

words.ar: منحدر زلق (خطوة تؤدي حتمًا إلى عواقب أسوأ)
words.ex: Some argue that editing genes to prevent disease is a slippery slope towards designer babies.
Strong legal safeguards are needed to protect people's private information.
Constant surveillance may infringe on citizens' right to privacy.
Is it morally justifiable to alter an embryo's DNA if it prevents a fatal illness?

dialogue.t: I've been reading about gene editing. Scientists can now potentially remove genes that cause inherited diseases before a baby is born.
It's fascinating, but it raises the question of whether we should be changing human DNA at all.
Ethically speaking, though, if you could prevent a child from suffering a terrible illness, wouldn't it be wrong not to?
In that case, maybe. But where do we draw the line between treating disease and enhancing intelligence or appearance?
That's the slippery slope argument. I'd say strict regulations and medical safeguards could prevent that.
Perhaps, but the implications of editing embryos are far-reaching. Those changes would be passed on to future generations who never gave their consent.
That's a strong point. So my position is that it's morally justifiable for preventing serious diseases, but only under very tight international controls.
I can accept that, as long as it's never available only to the wealthy. Otherwise it would deepen inequality.

grammar.title: Embedded (indirect) questions
grammar.ar: عندما ندمج سؤالًا داخل جملة أخرى مثل It raises the question of… أو I wonder… نستخدم ترتيب الجملة الخبرية (الفاعل ثم الفعل) وليس ترتيب السؤال، ولا نستخدم do/does/did. نستخدم whether (أو if) للأسئلة التي جوابها نعم أو لا، وأدوات الاستفهام مثل how وwhy للأسئلة الأخرى. بعد حرف الجر نستخدم whether وليس if.
examples: It raises the question of whether companies should be allowed to sell our data.
We need to consider how far scientists should be allowed to go.
Nobody can say for certain what the long-term consequences will be.

words.ex: There is a growing consensus that fossil fuels must be gradually phased out.
Our views diverged sharply on how quickly the transition should happen.
Solar power is an especially viable option in a country with so much sunshine.
Wind energy is intermittent, so it needs to be combined with reliable storage.
The transition to clean energy will require huge investment in new technology.
The overarching theme of the seminar was balancing economic growth with sustainability.

dialogue.t: We're almost out of time, so could someone summarise what we've discussed about renewable energy?
Sure. To sum up the key points, we looked at solar, wind and green hydrogen, and how realistic each one is for Saudi Arabia.
And what would you say the group agreed on?
The consensus seems to be that solar is the most viable option here, given the climate and the amount of available land.
Yes, I think everyone accepted that. Where opinions diverge is on the speed of the transition, isn't it?
Exactly. Some argued for a rapid shift, while others felt oil revenue is still needed to fund new projects. Broadly speaking, though, nobody denied that change is necessary.
And the issue of intermittent supply came up several times, too.
Right. What emerges from this is that investment in energy storage is just as important as building more solar farms.

grammar.title: Cleft sentences for emphasis
grammar.ar: الجمل المشطورة (cleft sentences) تُستخدم لإبراز فكرة معيّنة وتركيز انتباه السامع عليها، وهي شائعة جدًا عند التلخيص. النمط الأول يبدأ بـ What + جملة + is/was: What emerges is…. والنمط الثاني يبدأ بـ It is/was … that: It was solar power that…. ويمكن أيضًا استخدام Where أو The thing/The point في بداية الجملة.
examples: What most people agreed on was the need for better energy storage.
It was the cost of the transition that caused the most disagreement.
Where we differed was on how much the government should subsidise renewables.

words.ex: My main ambition is to study architecture abroad and eventually design sustainable buildings.
I've always been drawn to subjects that involve solving real-world problems.
Volunteering at the local library has been far more rewarding than I expected.
After a long day of revision, I usually unwind by playing football with my cousins.
If I had the chance, I'd pursue a career in medical research.
My parents encourage me to be well-rounded, so I balance my studies with sport and music.

dialogue.t: So, tell me a little about what you're studying at the moment.
To be honest, I've always been drawn to the sciences, so I'm focusing on biology and chemistry this year. They can be demanding, but I genuinely enjoy them.
And what do you enjoy most about your studies?
What I find particularly rewarding is when a difficult concept finally clicks. Last week we were studying genetics, and suddenly everything made sense. That feeling is hard to beat.
How do you usually spend your free time?
I'd say I'm the kind of person who needs a bit of balance, so I unwind by cycling along the coast or reading novels. It helps me clear my head before exams.
Is there anything you'd like to do in the future that you haven't done yet?
Definitely. If I had the chance, I'd spend a summer volunteering on a marine conservation project. It would combine my love of science with something practical and meaningful.

grammar.title: Present perfect with 'always' and second conditional
grammar.ar: نستخدم المضارع التام مع 'always' مثل I've always been drawn to للتعبير عن اهتمام بدأ في الماضي وما زال مستمراً حتى الآن، وهذا يجعل الإجابة أعمق من مجرد قول I like. أما الشرط الثاني (If + past simple, would + الفعل) فيُستخدم للحديث عن أمنيات أو مواقف افتراضية في المستقبل. تذكّر أن نقول If I had وليس If I would have، وهو خطأ شائع لدى المتحدثين بالعربية.
examples: I've always been fascinated by how languages develop over time.
If I had more free time, I'd learn to play the oud properly.
I've never really been interested in team sports, but I've always loved swimming.

words.ex: Both pictures depict students learning, but in very different settings.
The setting in the second photo looks far more relaxed than a traditional classroom.
Self-directed learning requires a great deal of discipline and motivation.
The students in the first photo seem to be involved in a collaborative project.
The boy at the front looks slightly apprehensive, as if he's about to present.
The first group is working outdoors, whereas the second is sitting in a lecture hall.

dialogue.t: Here are your pictures. They show people learning in different ways. Compare two of them and say how the people might be feeling and what challenges they might face.
Right. Both pictures depict people learning, but in quite contrasting situations. In the first one, they appear to be a group of teenagers on a field trip, examining plants in a forest.
It looks as though they're really engaged, and I'd imagine they might be feeling curious and energised because they're learning hands-on rather than from a textbook.
Unlike the other photo, which shows a young woman studying alone online late at night, there's a strong sense of teamwork here.
She seems rather tired, and I'd imagine she might be feeling a bit isolated. One challenge for her could be staying motivated without a teacher or classmates around.
Whereas the students outdoors might struggle to concentrate with so many distractions, so each way of learning has its own difficulties.
Thank you. Now, which of these ways of learning would you find more effective?

grammar.title: Describing impressions: appear to / look as though
grammar.ar: عندما نصف صورة ولا نكون متأكدين مما يحدث، نستخدم تراكيب تدلّ على الانطباع مثل appear to be + الفعل بصيغة -ing أو seem to be. ونستخدم look as though / look as if متبوعة بجملة كاملة فيها فاعل وفعل. لاحظ أن look يأتي بعده صفة مباشرة (She looks tired)، أما look like فيأتي بعده اسم. هذه التراكيب تُظهر للممتحن أنك تتكهّن بلغة دقيقة بدلاً من الجزم.
examples: They appear to be preparing for some kind of competition.
It looks as though the teacher has just asked a difficult question.
The girl on the left seems to be finding the task quite challenging.

words.ex: They could well be rehearsing for an end-of-year performance.
Judging by their smiles, they've just received some good news.
The boy seems completely engrossed in his experiment.
She could well be feeling frustrated because the equipment isn't working.
I'd go for the hands-on workshop because I remember things better when I do them myself.
It's hard to tell for sure, but they might be waiting for exam results.

dialogue.t: Your partner's pictures showed people learning practical skills. Which person do you think is enjoying the experience most?
It's hard to say for sure, but I'd go for the man learning to cook because he's laughing and seems really relaxed.
What about the girl learning to drive?
Judging by their expressions, she and her instructor are both quite tense. She could well be taking her first lesson, so she must be feeling a little nervous.
And which skill would you rather learn?
Personally, I'd find cooking more useful in the short term. I'm going to university soon, and I can't survive on sandwiches forever!
That's a fair point. Thank you.

grammar.title: Modals of deduction in the present
grammar.ar: نستخدم أفعال الاستنتاج للتعبير عن درجة يقيننا: must عندما نكون شبه متأكدين أن الأمر صحيح، وcan't عندما نكون شبه متأكدين أنه غير صحيح، وmight / may / could عندما يكون الأمر محتملاً فقط. وإضافة well بعد could أو might تزيد الاحتمال (could well = محتمل جداً). للحديث عن شيء يحدث الآن نستخدم modal + be + الفعل بصيغة -ing. انتبه: لا نستخدم mustn't للاستنتاج السلبي بل can't.
examples: They must be feeling proud after finishing such a difficult climb.
He can't be enjoying the lecture; he keeps checking his phone.
The woman might well be learning a new language for her job.

words.ex: Peer pressure can push teenagers to make choices they later regret.
A good teacher can become a powerful role model for young people.
Many teenagers are easily swayed by what they see on social media.
What's your take on the role of influencers in young people's lives?
Family values often shape our attitudes long before we realise it.
Teachers can raise students' aspirations by believing in their potential.

dialogue.t: Shall we start with family? I think parents have a huge influence, especially on decisions about education.
That's a good point, and building on that, I'd add that family values shape our choices even when we think we're being independent.
Exactly. What's your take on friends? Do you think peer pressure is as strong as people say?
I see it slightly differently. I think friends influence everyday choices, like clothes or hobbies, but not so much the big life decisions.
Interesting. Although some people do choose a university just because their friends are going there.
True, I hadn't thought of that. Shall we move on to the media? I'd say it sways young people more than anything else these days.
Possibly, but surely teachers still play a role as well, especially as role models?
Absolutely. A single inspiring teacher can completely change a student's aspirations.

grammar.title: Inviting opinions: direct and indirect questions
grammar.ar: في الجزء الثالث من الاختبار يجب أن تدعو شريكك للمشاركة، ويمكنك استخدام أسئلة مباشرة مثل What's your take on...? أو أسئلة غير مباشرة أكثر تهذيباً مثل I wonder what you think about... . في السؤال غير المباشر يكون ترتيب الكلمات كالجملة الخبرية (الفاعل ثم الفعل)، فنقول Do you know what he thinks وليس what does he think. كما تُستخدم الأسئلة الذيلية مثل isn't it? لطلب الموافقة.
examples: What's your take on the influence of advertising?
I'd be interested to know whether you think teachers are still influential.
Social media plays a bigger role than it used to, doesn't it?

words.ex: We need to narrow down the list to just two factors.
After a short discussion, we settled on family and the media.
I could agree to that, provided that we mention online influence specifically.
In my view, the influence of family outweighs that of friends.
Choosing teachers and media seems like a reasonable compromise.
It took a while, but we finally reached a consensus.

dialogue.t: Now you have a minute to decide which two factors are the most influential.
So, it seems we both agree that family is one of the strongest influences, don't we?
Yes, definitely. For the second one, I'd choose friends, because teenagers spend so much time with them.
Hmm, I'd argue the media outweighs friends, since much of what friends talk about comes from social media anyway.
I could go along with that, provided that we include social media and not just television or newspapers.
That makes sense. If we had to narrow it down, family and social media seem to shape the most important decisions.
Agreed. Let's settle on family and the media then.

grammar.title: Conditions with provided that, as long as, unless
grammar.ar: نستخدم provided (that) و as long as بمعنى 'بشرط أن'، وهي أقوى وأكثر رسمية من if، ومفيدة جداً عند التفاوض. أما unless فتعني 'إلا إذا' أي if not. بعد هذه الروابط نستخدم المضارع البسيط حتى عند الحديث عن المستقبل، فنقول provided that we agree وليس provided that we will agree.
examples: I'm happy to choose teachers, provided that we explain why they matter.
We can go with your suggestion as long as we keep family on the list.
Unless you have a strong objection, let's choose the media.

words.ex: Very few people today are truly self-sufficient.
We live in an interconnected world where events in one country affect everyone.
To a large extent, our opinions are shaped by the people around us.
As technology develops, we inevitably become more dependent on it.
It's a nuanced issue, so a simple yes or no wouldn't do it justice.
Even the most independent people rely on others for food, transport and healthcare.

dialogue.t: Is it possible to be truly independent in today's world?
There's no simple answer to that, but I'd say it largely depends on what we mean by independence.
Could you explain what you mean?
On the one hand, we can be independent thinkers and make our own decisions. On the other, we inevitably rely on others for almost everything we use, from food to the internet.
So do you think technology makes us less independent?
I'd go so far as to say that it makes us more dependent than any previous generation. Most of us couldn't find our way across a city without a phone.
That's an interesting point. Is that necessarily a bad thing?
Not entirely. All things considered, being interconnected has huge advantages, as long as we keep some basic skills and think critically.

grammar.title: Balancing arguments: while, although, whereas
grammar.ar: في الجزء الرابع يتوقّع الممتحن إجابات متوازنة تعرض أكثر من وجهة نظر. نستخدم although و while لربط فكرتين متعارضتين في جملة واحدة، ويمكن أن تأتي في بداية الجملة أو وسطها. أما whereas فتُستخدم غالباً لمقارنة شيئين مختلفين بشكل مباشر. تجنّب الجمع بين although و but في الجملة نفسها، وهو خطأ شائع لأن العربية تسمح بـ 'رغم أن... إلا أن...'.
examples: Although young people are more connected than ever, many feel surprisingly lonely.
While technology saves us time, it also makes us dependent on it.
Older generations valued self-sufficiency, whereas today we value collaboration.
